It is finally time to talk about the impact of fluctuating hormones

New Scientist August 19, 2026

The first rule of hormones was always that you don’t talk about your hormones. For decades, women have often felt the need to minimise or hide the impact that fluctuating levels of female sex hormones can have. The shifts in oestrogen levels experienced by many can be as profound as they are frequent – fluctuating monthly and also changing dramatically during puberty, pregnancy and menopause.

These hormonal ups and downs don’t just have a personal impact, but are also a nuisance for medical research, where it was long common to exclude women from studies to prevent their hormones from muddying the results.

One consequence of this exclusion was the view of ADHD as a male condition, particularly one involving hyperactive young boys. We now know that girls are just as likely as boys to have ADHD, but their symptoms can be harder to spot. Women who slipped under the radar as children are only now realising that they have the condition and seeking treatment.

Advertisement

Here again, hormones play a role, as scientists uncover what many women with ADHD already feel: that hormonal fluctuations and shifts can profoundly affect ADHD symptoms, sometimes undermining treatments and pushing their coping techniques to breaking point.

Hormonal fluctuations and shifts can profoundly affect ADHD symptoms and treatments

The hope, of course, is that a better understanding of how sex hormones affect brain function will lead to better treatments, but as we report, this work also gives women with ADHD a powerful self-understanding, finally allowing them to predict and work around changes in attention and motivation.

Yet how will those who most need to know ever find out? Mercifully, the taboo on talking about hormones has now been smashed, a surprisingly positive outcome of social media’s obsession with female health and wellness. What once felt unmentionable is now far from it, with hormone changes, menstrual phases and associated symptoms now commonly discussed online. The challenge is to use these conversations for progress and resist reverting back to old stereotypes.

Roie Galitz2026 World Press Photo Contest

Dwarfed by her dinner, a female polar bear feasts on the carcass of a sperm whale more than 100 times her mass, a deep-diving giant weighing more than 35 tonnes and usually found far below the ocean’s surface.

This shot, Polar Bear on Sperm Whale, was captured by Roie Galitz, and is one of the winners of the 2026 World Press Photo Contest. The image was taken from a small boat, using a drone. “Its unusual perspective and scale provoke curiosity and wonder, turning the frame into a visual and conceptual study of nature,” said the competition’s jury in an announcement about Galitz’s win.

Advertisement

The male sperm whale carcass makes for an unusual snack when compared with polar bears’ more typical seal meal. The location of the shot is also intriguing – captured in the polar pack ice north of the Norwegian archipelago of Svalbard, the shallow sea is far from the open-ocean trenches sperm whales usually inhabit. According to conservation organisation Polar Bears International, while most whales sink after dying, gas production during decomposition causes roughly 10 per cent of them to become buoyant, and their carcasses drift into shallower seas.

Although visually captivating, the shot acts as a stark reminder of the devastating effects Arctic warming is having on polar bears. Despite the bears’ best efforts at adaptation, their melting habitat presents a bleak outlook, with numbers expected to significantly decline before 2100.

The image can be seen as part of the World Press Photo Exhibition, at the MPB Gallery in London until 30 September.

The wild, gripping story of the psychedelic secreted by desert toads

New Scientist August 19, 2026

The Ego TripKimon de Greef, White Rabbit (UK); Doubleday (US)

If you have heard tales of 5-MeO-DMT, the psychedelic substance secreted by desert toads, then chances are it is due to one man. The Ego Trip tells the story of physician Octavio Rettig Hinojosa, who popularised the use of this intense drug, claiming it could treat addiction and trauma. He portrays 5-MeO-DMT as an ancient practice of the Seri people in Sonora, Mexico, and preaches its therapeutic benefits to his many disciples, promising it can reveal new planes of enlightenment.

Only, as Kimon de Greef writes, Rettig Hinojosa’s narrative is full of fiction, and his supposedly healing practices are described in the book as dark and dangerous. (De Greef is an acquaintance as we both report on psychedelics, and he thanks me in his acknowledgements for “inspiration and camaraderie”, as we received the same reporting grant.)

As de Greef writes, 5-MeO-DMT (in full, 5-methoxy-N, N-dimethyltryptamine), has been called the “Everest” of psychedelics. Whereas LSD distorts reality, creating vivid hallucinations, 5-MeO-DMT completely shatters all perception and sense of the self. The experience is brief, lasting less than half an hour, but creates a total obliteration of the ego. The psychedelic is found in Sonoran desert toads, and de Greef opens his book by describing, in graphic detail, how to extract the toxin. “One presses hard on their glands, which discharge explosively, like pimples,” he writes.

LSD distorts reality, creating vivid hallucinations, while 5-MeO-DMT shatters all sense of the self

This practice is ancient, says Rettig Hinojosa, having once been performed (but forgotten) by the Seri people. His work was initially welcomed by the group’s elders, and many of the Seri became 5-MeO-DMT practitioners. The importance of Indigenous customs are often heralded by psychedelic enthusiasts, who hark back to ancient ceremonies, but, in the case of 5-MeO-DMT, de Greef convincingly argues, there’s all too little evidence. Rettig Hinojosa latched on to the idea as an outsider, changing how the Seri are seen and their view of their history, but the relationship is shallow and the notion of ancestral toad psychedelics is a modern invention. A lot of Seri people have since distanced themselves from Rettig Hinojosa, asking him to stop using their name to champion the drug.

It gets worse. De Greef spends a lot of time with Rettig Hinojosa, whom he initially depicts as charismatic but dubious, only to show him act with increasing disregard towards those he gives drugs to. At one point, he claims, Rettig Hinojosa physically wrestles with a customer to get him to take more 5-MeO-DMT, and angrily commands a 14-year-old boy to inhale another hit. The psychedelic can cause people to lose consciousness, vomit and feel intense confusion and fear.

On another occasion, the book tells of Rettig Hinojosa pushing a woman who was bleeding and covered in mud while on the drug into a swimming pool with his foot. He paid her little regard as she emerged, dripping. Incredibly, de Greef admits that Rettig Hinojosa tricked him into taking psychedelics while reporting, after falsely telling him the substance was essential oil.

Though the subject is often dark, the writing itself has unexpectedly beautiful lines throughout: Sonoran toads have “pale bellies the girth of softballs”. I never thought I’d have such appreciation for these poor toads, who keep being plucked from their waddling lives and squeezed for their venom.

The narrative weaves together history and true crime – but there are also fascinating explorations of the science, from chemists creating the synthetic versions of 5-MeO-DMT, to the ecology of desert toads. We also hear about the impact of toad poaching on the communities who take part in the practice to feed the growing drug trade.

The book’s pacing stays sharp, and there are plenty of moments of high tension – not least when de Greef ends a chapter by introducing a lawyer who had just helped Rettig Hinojosa avoid a murder charge. Throughout, as de Greef notes, Rettig Hinojosa denies any wrongdoing.

The reporting is diligent, and de Greef even manages to join a toad-poaching expedition. 5-MeO-DMT is cheap to synthesise, he explains, but there is demand for the natural substance, with many users believing they are taking an Indigenous sacrament. The practice is ugly, though, disturbing the toads and often involving child labour. Many conservationists and prominent figures in the psychedelics field have called for an end to the drug’s collection.

De Greef’s expedition involved a teenager whose brothers are missing, presumed dead – two people among the 100,000 forcibly disappeared by cartels and state security forces over the past 20 years. Sometimes, the boy joins a non-profit founded by his mother to help find the remains of victims. “By day, he searches for bodies,” his mother chillingly tells de Greef. “At night, he searches for toads.”

Having traced Rettig Hinojosa’s journey and how his “guru” status enabled 5-MeO-DMT’s rise, the book’s final section explores its commodification. Why would a drug that causes such terror and physical reactions be considered a potential medicine? Because it is quick. Other psychedelics like psilocybin create trips lasting at least 6 hours, but the effects of 5-MeO-DMT can last for just 15 minutes, making it far cheaper and easier to roll out.

Contemporary supporters of psychedelics included the late Amanda Feilding, the aristocrat who funded much research on the substances in the UK, and the late Bill Atkinson – the renowned Apple engineer who, de Greef discovers, invented a bespoke 5-MeO-DMT vape pen, which he gave out for free. Despite this enthusiasm, no medical use for the drug has been proven and 5-MeO-DMT is still illegal in the US, UK and elsewhere.

Incredibly, though, it has had impressive results in clinical trials as a medication for treatment-resistant depression. But de Greef suggests the data may not capture the full story: some participants may be more distressed after the experience than the results reflect.

After reading de Greef’s book, 5-MeO-DMT seems like a questionable mental health cure –and certainly not one that should be taken with “gurus”. The Ego Trip, though, is compelling, guiding us through the dangerous industries and characters surrounding this supposedly ego-dissolving drug.

Dreamland: The true tale of America’s opiate epidemic by Sam Quinones

Vivid on-the-ground reporting exposes the extensive pharmaceutical supply of opioids, while also showing how a small group in Nayarit, Mexico, created a pipeline of black-tar heroin to the US.

How to Change Your Mind: The new science of psychedelics by Michael Pollan

Anyone interested in psychedelics should start with journalist Michael Pollan’s book, which chronicles their history, and explores the scientific evidence that these drugs can have powerful therapeutic effects.

Poacher: Confessions from the abalone underworld by Kimon de Greef and Shuhood Abader

De Greef’s first book was about illegal shellfish trading. Another excellent piece of writing, it looks at how criminal syndicates extract money from those doing the actual diving, smuggling the wares to luxury markets.

Empire of the Mind: The battle for the future of psychedelic medicine by Olivia Goldhill

A cheeky extra – but my forthcoming book looks at psychedelic medical research, and the power of the healthcare industry to change our understanding of mental illness.

This sci-fi novel is a riveting tale of an oppressive galactic empire

New Scientist August 19, 2026

The Infinite StateRichard Swan, Gollancz (UK); Tor Books (US)

In The Infinite State by Richard Swan, the vast Decurion Empire is governed by Pater Aeternus. It’s a political system that feels like a mash-up of Nazi Germany, Soviet Russia and Rome under its most oppressive emperors – except that this state has spaceships and runs a chunk of the galaxy. The author also throws in a hard-drinking cop and some murder mysteries for good measure. While that might sound like a mess, the novel is anything but.

In the capital city of Kada Gamar, Pater Aeternus, aka the Party, rules without pity. Women are second-class citizens, prized only for their fertility, and the suppressed masses are kept happy with a futuristic version of the Roman circus, involving a racing sport called “hypersledding”.

Advertisement

Katherine Fuller is the first of our three main protagonists. When her extremely wealthy husband dies in mysterious circumstances, Katherine is left with a great deal of money but also a growing unease about the way her home planet is ruled. She decides to spend her billions on the purchase of a far-flung planet where she intends to establish a democracy. But why would the Party ever let her do such a thing?

Our second protagonist is the aforementioned cop. Inspektor Cyprian Reis is a good guy, albeit capable of serious violence, but he is on his last legs. In a world where murder is often the most convenient solution to bureaucratic problems, at least as far as the Party is concerned, Cyprian keeps going because the state holds his children hostage. Now he is dealing with a dead body that has the hallmarks of a political killing, but with some worrying oddities, and things are about to get very complicated.

The suppressed masses are kept happy with a futuristic Roman Circus sport called hypersledding

Thirdly, we have Julian Yashego. He’s from outside the Decurion Empire but has been brought in from the distant planet of Trillia to win races for the Party… for reasons that are not at all clear. Julian appears to be the focus of a great deal of machination, but why are the Party’s big bads so concerned with a dim-witted hypersled driver?

One of the great joys of this book is how wonderful its villains are. My favourite is Jaroslav Droor, the minister of information, who reminds me of the wonderful torturer, Sand dan Glokta, in Joe Abercrombie’s The Blade Itself. What is clear from the start is that these high-ups in the Party, each viler than the last, aren’t exactly rowing in the same direction.

I won’t ruin the book by revealing more, but I can say it is thoroughly enjoyable, with plots nesting within plots, and machinations within machinations. It’s well designed and well thought through; no loose threads here.

I do have a few small comments, though. Katherine, the only female lead protagonist, is strangely feeble in a crisis. She’s also not much more than a pawn, plot-wise, which is irritating.

Second, this book is mainly people talking to each other. You don’t really get much of a sense of the physicality of the planets the action takes place on. Personally, I don’t mind, but just a heads-up that this is a very talky book.

Finally, I think the ending is a bit neat and sweet. I worry that people won’t feel much need to read on in what is intended to be a series. But perhaps I’m wrong about that.

Niggles aside, this is a clever, inventive and satisfying book, and hats off to its author. I look forward to more of the Decurion Empire’s revolting offspring.

The Blade ItselfJoe Abercrombie, Gollancz (UK); Orbit (US)This is fantasy, or at least at the more fantastical end of the fantasy-sci-fi spectrum. However, since I mentioned it in the main review, I feel justified in recommending it to anyone who hasn’t already feasted upon it. It’s Abercrombie’s debut, but wow, is it assured.

Emily H. Wilson is the author of the Sumerians series (Inanna, Gilgamesh and Ninshubar, all published by Titan) and she is currently working on her first sci-fi novel. She is a former editor of New Scientist and you can follow her on Instagram @emilyhwilson1

Mount Maunganui landslide: Business owners respond to council’s external review

New Zealand Herald August 19, 2026

Tauranga City Council's external review into the fatal Mauao landslide found more than 20 years of known landslide risk led to a "preventable" tragedy. Main image / Jason Dorday, inset / Alyse Wright

A Mount Maunganui business owner has accused Tauranga City Council of a “she’ll-be-right” mentality before January’s landslide tragedy.

Six holidaymakers were killed after a section of Mauao collapsed into the council-owned Mount Maunganui Beachside Holiday Park at about 9.30am on January 22 during record rainfall.

The findings of the council’s external review into the landslide, prepared by retired High Court Judge Paul Davison, KC, were released yesterday.

Davison found the council “missed several opportunities” to evacuate campers to safety in a “preventable” disaster.

His review found more than two decades of recorded landslide risk to the campground and found that systemic issues within the council failed to ensure these were properly managed.

The council has committed to implementing Davison’s recommendations, and its leaders have acknowledged the organisation had failed to properly manage risk at the campground over many years.

Rustica Pizzeria is located on Adams Ave opposite the campground but has closed “indefinitely” after seven challenging months following the slip.

Owner Michele Delaini said he believed the council had a “she’ll be right” mentality and in his opinion had “paid the price with the lives of six people”.

In his view: “I’ve done what I had to do to minimise the risk in my business. They [the council] didn’t do anything to minimise their risk.”

Davison said the hazard was not unknown and that, had a Trigger Action Response Plan (Tarp) been in place as experts had recommended, it would have prompted an evacuation and the victims would not have been in the path of the landslide.

“The loss of life could in all likelihood have been averted.”

However, the review did not determine civil, criminal or disciplinary liability, and Davison made no finding that any individual caused the deaths.

“It does not find that any individual did anything intentionally or deliberately wrong, or that any one or more persons’ acts or omissions caused these tragic deaths.”

Delaini said more lives would have been lost if Lisa Maclennan, a Morrinsville teacher who died in the landslide, hadn’t warned people to evacuate.

Delaini told the Bay of Plenty Times he closed his pizzeria this month following further slippage at the campground site in July and the repeated closures of Adams Ave.

These are part of a landslide risk management process the council introduced after the January slip.

Delaini said he understood why the council was being cautious.

However, he said the council appeared to have done little about landslide risk for decades.

“They are trying to patch up whatever hasn’t been done for the last 25 years.”

Beach Hut Cafe owner Michelle Craig said the preventability of the slip tragedy was “horrifying” and “re-traumatising”.

“I couldn’t be more devastated.”

Craig said the council needed to “do better”.

She said she would like to see an evaluation of the council’s response to affected businesses after the tragedy.

Tauranga Business Chamber chief executive Matt Cowley said the review would be difficult news for Mount Maunganui businesses.

He said they were already facing prolonged disruption and “holding on for a really good summer”.

Cowley said Adams Ave businesses could face restrictions for another two years, adding to the financial pressure they had faced since the slip.

He said businesses relied heavily on foot traffic generated by Mauao, with its popular scenic walking tracks.

“Their rents are based on a million people walking around Mauao. With that significantly dropped off, that’s a lot of overheads and costs they have to bear.”

He said businesses had hoped remediation work on Mauao’s walking tracks would bring visitors back, but they now expected delays.

Cowley said businesses needed to work closely with suppliers, manage their finances carefully, and think creatively as they navigated the uncertainty.

“It’s a game of inches really at the moment … it’s gritting through.”

Bijou Johnson is a multimedia journalist based in Bay of Plenty. A passionate writer and reader, she grew up in Tauranga and developed a love for journalism while exploring various disciplines at university. She holds a Bachelor of Arts in Classical Studies from Massey University.

Christopher Luxon Christchurch meeting disrupted by protesters

New Zealand Herald August 19, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon visited Christchurch for a public meeting last night, as the campaign trail for November’s election heats up. Herald senior journalist Mike Thorpe reports from a raucous and fractious event.

Christopher Luxon must have expected some opposition in Christchurch when his visit was first planned, not least of all from the residents of Pegasus, in North Canterbury.

Just last month, a delegation had travelled to Parliament to present a petition of 16,000 signatures opposing the use of the Fast-track Act to turn their town’s golf course into a residential development of 1000 homes.

But just hours before Luxon took the stage at Addington Raceway, that application from Wolfbrook Residential, the current owners of the former championship golf course, was declined by Infrastructure Minister Chris Bishop.

The convoy from north of the Waimakariri River was called off, and the Prime Minister could surely have expected a quieter conversation with the 450 people who gathered for Wednesday night’s public meeting.

Not so. An orchestrated protest event interrupted the Prime Minister on six separate occasions across multiple issues – leading the MC and Minister for Tourism, Louise Upston, to ask if anyone else wanted to speak out before being kicked out.

Even before the Prime Minister took the stage – or the crowd filed in, veteran activist John Minto aimed his megaphone at the entrance. Whilst he didn’t make it inside, his pro-Palestine supporters did.

But it was a climate protester who was first to find his voice, comparing the plans for the Denniston Plateau to a landmark of Middle Earth.

“We are Mordor,” he screamed as he was ushered out shortly after Luxon’s opening speech began. His exit prompted another to stand and continue the climate change message.

He, too, was removed before Luxon picked up where he left off, delivering his assessment of New Zealand’s economy and the difficulties it has faced with worldwide events. The mention of global politics sparked another protester with another cause.

“Genocide in Gaza!” yelled the next protester from the middle of the crowd.

“You’ve disgraced New Zealand, blood on your hands!”

The crowd grew restless when the fifth interruption came with a call to “sanction Israel”.

Shortly after Upston’s invitation to speak up, and Luxon’s oratory resumption, another voice momentarily found the courage to voice her discontent with New Zealand’s foreign affairs.

But she fluffed her rehearsed lines. Deflated, she voluntarily turned for the exit before security arrived at her row, delivering a half-hearted “sanction Israel” as the audience groaned with displeasure.

Luxon was largely unperturbed by the intrusions – though he was also questionable in his delivery. He recounted a recent dinner table discussion with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi that apparently started with “Narendra, what’s going on in India?”

He rolled out statistics and anecdotes that supported his claims that the current government has delivered on crime reduction and is boosting education. The apparent achievements were celebrated with enthusiastic applause – like his assertion that ram raids are down 85%.

Luxon also spoke about the amount the previous government had borrowed before suggesting that it was possibly beyond the crowd’s comprehension. He says “it’s late” and the crowd had “glazed over”, going, “Chris, I don’t understand millions or billions”. For the record, it was 7.45pm, and the crowd appeared to be quite familiar with those numerical values.

The evening finished with roughly half a dozen questions that ranged from rates caps to Covid vaccines and eventually that potentially sticky subject – Fast-track.

Luxon wouldn’t speak directly about Pegasus, but he did defend the intent of Fast-track legislation.

The Prime Minister had arrived on stage at 7.25pm, and by 8.16pm, the public meeting was all over.

The Prime Minister’s Office says that he hung around speaking to people until 9.30pm.

It was a busy night for Luxon – but a busier night for security.

Mike Thorpe is a senior multimedia journalist for the Herald, based in Christchurch. He has been a broadcast journalist across television and radio for 20 years and joined the Herald in August 2024.

Mount Maunganui landslide: Davison report prompts calls for action, accountability

New Zealand Herald August 19, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Tauranga MP Sam Uffindell says a “huge question mark has to hang over” the future of the council’s chief executive in light of the review into the Mauao tragedy that claimed six lives.

“This is a massive problem,” he told Newstalk ZB’s Ryan Bridge Early Edition.

“We’ve got a very tragic situation where six people have lost their lives in a preventable situation due to systemic failure within the organisation. And a huge question mark has to hang over the CEO.“

Uffindell said he was yet to read through the full report but noted there were several others underway, including a Government inquiry.

“I don’t want to preempt those processes. I want to understand all the findings and ensure accountability where it belongs.”

The release of the first review into the fatal Mount Maunganui landslide has prompted calls for accountability and action.

The review, led by Paul Davison, KC, found the tragedy was “preventable” and identified systemic failures within Tauranga City Council spanning more than two decades.

Six people died when the landslide from Mauao hit the council-owned campground at its foot about 9.30am on January 22 after record rain.

Today chief executive Marty Grenfell said he was never made aware of any risk to life or risk of slips at Mauao in the eight years he’d led the organisation.

He refused to say whether he’d offered or considered resigning as a result.

Speaking on Ryan Bridge TODAY, Grenfell described the report as “accurate”, “damning and “confronting” but rejected the idea that it was unfair on him as the council’s leader.

“The reason for commissioning this report was to get early information in order to act and make changes.

”My focus is to do that. I’ve been involved with this organisation for eight years. I know it better than anybody. I’m best placed to drive the changes that Mr Davison has highlighted."

Grenfell said the reports done on Mauao and provided to the council’s operational arm came from as early as 1999, and he was not made aware of them until they surfaced in online searches following the tragedy.

Asked whether that was indicative of problems within the organisation’s leadership, Grenfell stressed it was “a systems issue”.

“The systems have been in place for a long time ... Obviously, we failed in this situation.”

Local Government Minister Simon Watts said he now wants to review other councils across New Zealand in light of the report to ensure each has the appropriate systems and processes to access and act on information at hand.

“When it’s preventable, it hurts even more,” Watts told Ryan Bridge TODAY.

“We need to get assurance from councils across the country that the problems that have been identified in Tauranga don’t exist on a more widespread issue across the country.“

He said the fact that there was prior knowledge of risk to life at Mauao, but no processes and systems in place to monitor and regulate them, was “the failure of this sad, very sad circumstance“.

“As Minister for Local Government, I’ll be seeking assurance that that risk and process doesn’t exist across other parts of councils and other parts of the country.”

Tauranga Mayor Mahé Drysdale called the report “confronting” – particularly its finding that there had been multiple lost opportunities to act.

He had personally apologised to the families, telling them “this is unacceptable from our organisation”, he told Newstalk ZB’s Mike Hosking Breakfast.

“The clear thing here is we’ve got to make sure any report that comes in tells us there’s a risk of life, it’s escalated up the organisation so we can manage it.”

Mount Maunganui resident Colin McGonagle told the Herald he was “frustrated and disappointed” by what he viewed as the lack of personal accountability from senior leaders at Tauranga City Council after the report.

Two of the geotechnical reports emphasising the risk to life were commissioned recently, in December 2023 and June 2025 respectively.

“Frustration and definitely disappointment – recent reports that have been ignored. At what point is somebody held accountable?” McGonagle said.

He understood the review found safety warnings were not heeded because of organisational failures, but believed leadership responsibility should rest with Grenfell and Drysdale.

Both leaders have committed to seeing the council implement Davison’s recommendations.

Davison’s review found no individual accountable for the tragedy.

McGonagle took photos of small slips, water rushing down the bank, and an image of the campground manager and a council staff member on a golf buggy at 7.40am on the day of the disaster.

The images helped the review team build a timeline of what happened.

He was confident the Mount would open again, given it was a treasure to thousands of locals.

“It’s their ritual, it’s their church for a lot of people here. It’s where they get healing, walking up there and walking around it. It’s a blessing,” he said.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said the Government needed to act “immediately” to prevent a repeat of the tragedy.

In a statement to the Herald, Hipkins said: “The Government needs to take this review and act immediately to ensure a tragedy like this never happens again.

“Too often, after disasters, we hear promises that lessons will be learned. The real test is whether governments and councils actually act on those lessons.”

Bay of Plenty MP Tom Rutherford said the findings were “deeply confronting” and the focus now needed to be on addressing the systemic failures identified in the review.

“People rightly expect councils to put public safety first.”

Rutherford said accountability mattered but he was not interested in rushing to conclusions about whether individuals, including Grenfell, should resign.

He welcomed the council accepting all of the review’s recommendations and said he would be watching to ensure they were acted on.

Rutherford said the Government’s separate inquiry into the landslide would consider the review alongside other evidence before reaching its own conclusions.

He said legislative changes could be considered if the inquiry identified a need for them.

Rutherford also backed reopening Mauao when it was safe to do so, and said the future of the campground should be considered by the council in consultation with the community.

Tauranga MP Sam Uffindell said he was not surprised the review found systemic failure within Tauranga City Council.

He said the public would expect accountability but he wanted to read the full report and consider the Government’s separate inquiry before drawing conclusions about individual responsibility.

Uffindell said it was now up to the council to properly implement the review’s recommendations and he acknowledged people who felt disappointed by missed warning signs had every “right to feel let down”.

“The thoughts of everyone need to be with the families and the loved ones of those who are no longer here today because of the tragic circumstances.”

Act’s local MP Cameron Luxton said the review answered important questions about the events leading up to “that terrible day”.

“I hope this report provides some answers for the families of those who died.”

He said Mount Maunganui businesses were still waiting for clarity about what happens next.

Luxton said businesses had lost trade, with some “barely hanging on” and others having closed.

He said more clarity was needed about what work remained on Mauao, who was responsible for it, and when access could be restored.

“People understand Mauao cannot reopen until it is safe. What we need is more light on a plan for getting access back.”

Rotorua Mayor Tania Tapsell acknowledged Tauranga City Council’s “open and honest” response to the review and said all councils should learn from its findings.

“While our Rotorua council has not yet had the opportunity to fully review the report, I accept the challenge and request from Mayor Mahé [Drysdale] to ensure this tragedy prompts all councils and other organisations across New Zealand to learn from this.”

She said the Rotorua Lakes Council had processes in place to identify and manage natural hazard risks.

“However, we are now committed to reviewing our own risk assessments and management processes to ensure we remain confident that appropriate safeguards are in place for our communities and visitors.

“Our thoughts are with those still grieving the tragic loss of six lives in the Mauao landslide.”

Two Rotorua residents were among those lost.

The chairman of the Government inquiry into the fatal landslides in Tauranga, Sir Mark O’Regan, confirmed the inquiry will consider the Davison report, but noted the two had different terms of reference.

“The Government inquiry’s scope covers both the Mauao and Welcome Bay Rd landslides, and the actions of all relevant agencies, not just Tauranga City Council.”

O’Regan expressed sympathy to the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives, as well as to the injured and everyone affected by the January landslides.

WorkSafe central regional manager Nigel Formosa said the agency’s investigation was focused on “potential duties under the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015 prior to the landslide”.

It was considering material from the council and other sources, and would review Davison’s report.

“We will reach our own findings and determine next steps based on the evidence gathered through our investigation. It’s important that we don’t pre-empt any investigation outcomes.”

Formosa said WorkSafe’s investigation, which began in February, could take up to 12 months, with no further updates expected until later this year.

Bay of Plenty Police crime manager Detective Inspector Lindsay Pilbrow said the police investigation into the fatal landslides at Mount Maunganui and Welcome Bay Rd continued.

“We are also continuing to make inquiries on behalf of the coroner.

“Police’s family liaison officers remain in contact with the families, and our heartfelt thoughts are with those who lost their loved ones.”

Pilbrow said it would be inappropriate for police to comment further at this stage.

Number of 25C-plus days in Auckland could double by 2050, new research shows

New Zealand Herald August 19, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

By Kate Newton of RNZ

Longer, more frequent heatwaves in the country’s largest city could harm and even kill people if more is not done to prepare, heat researchers say.

Auckland Council has published research showing the number of hot days over 25C could double by 2050, under a moderate climate change scenario.

Further into the future, or under a more severe climate scenario, the number could increase by as much as five-fold.

The research also showed that heatwaves lasting weeks are a possibility in future – with often no reprieve at night-time either.

Council principal sustainability and resilience adviser Lauren Simpson said that at the moment, the longest heatwave during a hot summer was about four days.

“That will shift to the longest heat wave being about 20 days in 2090 under a high warming scenario, so really extended periods of hot weather,” she said.

“With that will come health impacts. That is compounded when you have consecutive hot nights as well, because long periods of hot days and hot nights mean that the body doesn’t have time or doesn’t have a reprieve from the heat.”

The new paper follows previous research the council published in 2024, showing that Auckland had an urban heat island effect – where the CBD and other highly urban areas were several degrees hotter than the rest of the city.

The latest research said that effect would compound future heat.

“Urban areas such as city centre show the greatest number of night-time heat events in summer, with the highest minimum temperatures. These areas are at greatest risk of adverse health impacts.”

The scenarios ranged from a low emissions pathway (SSP1) to a high emissions pathway (SSP3), using Auckland’s hottest summer to date – 2021 to 2022 – as a baseline.

“That wasn’t an average summer – we’re trying to look at the worst-case scenario,” Simpson said.

The research did not use the most extreme future scenario (SSP5), which the Government has criticised councils for including in their planning.

Recent heatwaves in Europe and Britain have been blamed for thousands of excess deaths and have fanned wildfires across the continent.

Simpson said heatwaves in New Zealand were still uncommon, but the research showed the need to prepare now.

“We haven’t yet experienced the kind of heat that we’re seeing in those other cities, and so they’re providing a really great opportunity to learn from, to see what works, because lots of those cities, they’re learning themselves.”

Before this summer and a strengthening ‘super El Nino’, the council was planning a campaign with advice for how to keep cool, she said.

“As part of that, we’re developing a cool spaces map that will help people locate cool spaces in their local communities and that might be shading parks or public facilities with air conditioning, local beaches, bottle refill stations, that sort of thing.”

Otago University professor Simon Hales, who has researched extreme heat for decades, said people could experience its effects after one day.

“But the effects on health are certainly greater if the heatwave is more prolonged – if there’s no relief at night and if it continues for several days,” he said.

That was likely because the physiological stress of extreme heat, as well as the environmental effects, slowly built up.

“People are getting maybe dehydrated as well as too hot – their bodies are not managing to keep up with the cooling, and our houses and infrastructure are gradually heating up more and more as the heatwave continues.”

Research Hales collaborated on in 2000 found that for every degree of heat over 20C, the mortality rate in Christchurch increased by 1%.

The methods in that research were cruder than subsequent research, but the link between extreme heat and excess deaths and hospitalisations had since been clearly established across hundreds, “maybe even thousands” of scientific papers, he said.

That included research in 2024 that found more preschoolers ended up in New Zealand hospitals on hot days.

Children, older people and those with existing health conditions were all vulnerable to heat, he said.

“Many of the main chronic health issues – things like cardiovascular disease, respiratory disease, psychiatric problems – many of these things are sensitive to heat in the short term, so you see increases in hospital admissions and deaths from those things.”

Heatwaves are defined as several consecutive days where temperatures fall in the top few per cent of what is considered normal for that time and place.

“It’s a little bit hard to understand at first glance,” Hales said.

“If you take the example of a city that’s in the north of Europe, people might start to have an increase in the health effects of heat at temperatures that we would consider to be quite comfortable,” he said.

“Likewise, people who live in tropical countries probably would not have any effect on their health at temperatures that we would start to be thinking, ‘this is getting pretty hot’.”

The preparation for future hot weather in New Zealand was “lagging a bit, but it’s not disastrous”.

“The more important question is, how’s our preparation for [mitigating] climate change at the moment? And I would give you a very different answer to that question – I think, as a country, we are going backwards.”

Simpson said creating more green space in urban areas could both mitigate climate change and help cities adapt to it.

“Not only do trees and plants help to cool our urban environment, but they provide a myriad of other benefits – from supporting our biodiversity, stormwater management, improving the aesthetics and connection for people with nature, and absorbing or sequestering carbon.”

There were additional things to consider in urban planning and development, such as using building and paving materials that reflected heat instead of absorbing it.

That included thinking about how homes were built, she said.

“In recent times we’ve made quite a good shift to making our homes warmer and drier. We now need to be thinking about making them cooler.”

Last year, Auckland Council and the New Zealand Green Building Council (NZGBC) sent a joint letter to the Government asking for changes to the Building Code, requiring new houses to pass a check at the design stage to ensure they would not overheat.

NZGBC chief executive Andrew Eagles said half of new builds now were terrace houses and apartments, and many of them were overheating too frequently.

“We don’t recess our windows, so you’re not shading that space. And at the same time we’ve had a love affair with very large glazing – and that so the combination of large glazing and no cross-ventilation and not recessing means the house just can’t get rid of all that heat.”

Many designs would require only minor tweaks, such as slightly smaller windows – which would save money too – and larger eaves, he said.

“It’s all things that can be manageable, but if you don’t have to do that check then the home is going to overheat for large parts of January, February, March, causing really significant discomfort.”

With the right design, it was possible to have a home that was both warm in winter and cool in summer, Eagles said.

“We need to destroy a myth that it’s one or the other.”

Vietnamese couple grew 460 cannabis plants opposite court house, near police station

New Zealand Herald August 19, 2026

A group of Vietnamese nationals managed to grow 460 cannabis plants under the noses of police and district court staff in a small Waikato town.

But Tu Ngoc Vu, his wife, Hong Thi Vu, and Thanh Van Mai, were ultimately busted by staff at a neighbouring daycare, who had noticed an odour radiating from the Huntly warehouse.

As well as using the 40m by 20m industrial warehouse on William St, the trio had a growing operation at their home on Duke St, Ngāruawāhia, where police found 60kg of cannabis plants, hundreds of grams of packaged head, soil and electrical items.

The couple appeared for sentence in the Hamilton District Court on Wednesday, charged with cultivating cannabis and possession of cannabis for supply.

Mai was jailed by Judge Arthur Tompkins for three years and nine months in May. The couple’s lawyer, Callum Fredric, aimed his submissions at getting his clients’ prison time below that.

After police were alerted to the smell of weed wafting from next door, officers executing a search warrant arrived to find the group working in the warehouse on July 4, 2024.

They had diverted the power, and like other similar operations, the warehouse had its carpet and doors removed, boards fastened to window frames to prevent light escaping, and flexible ducting connecting filters to fans to circulate air for ventilation and reduce the cannabis odour.

There were also filters and fans, underneath which sat artificial lighting and large pots filled with plants, all connected with an irrigation and plant feed system.

As well as the 460 plants, there was 41.5kg of saleable dried cannabis bud already harvested, and 103 50-litre bags of soil.

The trio were all found with cash on them; Mai $3750, Tu Vu $1700.80, and Hong Vu $5839.90 and A$580 ($699).

After speaking to their lawyers, they all refused to give police access to their phones.

But by the time police searched their Duke St property, it was apparent they’d tried to clear out some of the cannabis.

There were three standalone dwellings comprising a house, a shed with four makeshift rooms, one of which was made from a portable tent, and another shed.

In total, police found 61.079kg of cannabis there.

Police accepted the trio were not the principal protagonists, but were “significantly” involved as overseers of the operation and were motivated by financial gain.

Crown prosecutor Lexie Glaser urged the judge to sentence the couple in line with Mai, for whom he took a five-year jail starting point. Mai has filed an appeal of his sentence.

She accepted the couple should get credit for their guilty pleas and hardship as foreigners, but noted they had arrived in New Zealand in 2023 before offending the following year.

However, neither had shown any remorse and had instead minimised their actions, shifted blame and had a “dismissive attitude”.

Fredric pushed for a lower starting point of four years’ jail, and an end point of two years and nine months.

Although they offended over two premises, neither was “huge” and were instead two moderately sized operations.

The 60kg of plants seized from Duke St was not saleable, and once dried would have been “substantially lower” than that weight.

He said there was no evidence the Vus did anything other than grow and tend to the plants.

“It’s not clear what type of operational role they held beyond just growing the plants and tending to the plantation,” he said.

In his affidavit to the court, Tu Vu said he’d paid $40,000 to an agent to move to New Zealand for work only to find that he’d been scammed and there was no job available.

“Out of financial desperation, owing a lot of money, he has accepted work as a cannabis labourer,” Fredric said.

He said the foreign hardship would be harder on the pair because they wouldn’t be able to ring each other as they would be housed in separate prisons.

They were also away from their three children and were keen to be deported back to Vietnam at the end of their stint behind bars.

Contact the Open Justice team

Judge Tompkins said while the pair had been assessed as being at low risk of reoffending, there had been limited or no remorse shown, particularly by Tu Vu.

He accepted the pair had significant roles in the operation but that there were others higher up in the chain.

“These three defendants were not ... principal antagonists in the cultivation,” the judge said.

“Having said that, this was a significant operation with a high degree of premeditation.”

The judge ultimately accepted the pair were lower down the hierarchy than Mai, so took a starting point of four years and three months’ jail.

After applying credits for their guilty pleas and personal mitigating factors, Judge Tompkins jailed them both for three years.

He also ordered forfeiture of the cash they were each found with.

Belinda Feek is an Open Justice reporter based in Waikato. She has worked at NZME for 11 years and has been a journalist for 22.

Five-star Napier lodging The County Hotel has cancelled customers’ room bookings amid a receivership process at the venue.

One customer was informed on Wednesday that he would not be refunded for his two-night booking at the end of August, which cost more than $400, and would need to rebook elsewhere.

He was advised to try to reverse the payment through his bank, as he only made the booking last week.

The County Hotel is located in the Napier CBD and is a five-star boutique hotel with 18 rooms, an “intimate library” and function areas, according to its website.

The three-storey hotel also features a bar and restaurant called Churchill’s.

Future bookings have been suspended on the hotel’s website and Churchill’s Lounge Bar and Restaurant has closed.

The County Hotel is owned and operated through two companies, The Barons Ltd and Barons Operations Ltd, which entered receivership last week.

Those companies are owned by Angela and Christopher Barons.

Angela declined to comment when contacted by Hawke’s Bay Today and forwarded inquiries to the receiver.

A representative for the appointed receiver, BDO Christchurch, also declined to comment at this stage.

The receivers were appointed by Heartland Bank, according to a notice.

The hotel has been placed on the market on a couple of occasions in recent years but according to property records has failed to sell.

Just last week, Auckland resident Hamish Williams booked a two-night stay for the end of August through the hotel’s website, paying just over $400 for a room for him and his wife.

The booking was made two days before the sister companies went into receivership.

The receivers called him on Wednesday morning to explain the situation.

“They explained to me that the company had been placed in receivership, and my booking would not be able to go through and that they would be unable to refund it.

“However, they did say you can try and reverse the charge through your bank, so I have begun that process.

“They [also] gave me recommendations of where else I could stay in Napier, which I thought was a nice touch.”

He said he and his wife were “lucky it was only two nights” and they would rebook elsewhere, as they were coming to Napier to watch their daughter’s football tournament.

“More than anything, it is really sad to hear this has happened.

“It was a wonderful place and a unique offering on a national scale, I would say.”

Williams said they stayed at the hotel for their anniversary two years ago and loved it.

“It was what you’d call memorable.

“It was a warm reception; we felt it had a real personal touch.

“The owner told us the story about the business ... and she really sold us on the place.

“So, coming back to stay there again was an easy choice. We had such a good time.”

He said they even had a brandy room, which he had enjoyed during a tour of the hotel.

Constructed in 1909, the building was home to the Hawke’s Bay County Council for almost 80 years, until it was restored and repurposed into its current use as a hotel and eatery in 1993.

The building survived the 1931 earthquake.

Teenage ace Rafael Jódar endures defeat by Cobolli but his star is rising

The Guardian Wed, 19 Aug 2026 21:33:39 GMT

Spaniard loses narrowly in fourth round of the Cincinnati Open yet the buzz around him will only get louder

As Rafael Jódar slowly trudged from the court, he could only bring himself to wave at his adoring crowd for no more than a millisecond. The 19-year-old was appropriately devastated after he had come within two points of victory on numerous occasions before losing 4-6, 7-6 (3), 6-3 in the fourth round of the Cincinnati Open to an excellent Flavio Cobolli.

No matter, Jódar departs Ohio having further solidified himself as the subject of so much conversation on the ATP Tour. This has been a turbulent and unpredictable year in men’s tennis, largely thanks to Carlos Alcaraz’s extended injury layoff. The one certainty through it all has been the imperious rise of Jódar. After a short period competing at the University of Virginia, Jódar started to play regularly on the tour only in May last year. In August 2025, he was ranked No 540. He began the 2026 season at No 165.

Over the past four months, Jódar has won his first ATP title in Marrakech, he reached another final in Washington, he powered to his first grand slam quarter-final at Roland Garros and at Masters 1000 level he has reached a semi-final and two quarter-finals.

With the exception of the grass-court season, where he struggled with an abdominal strain, Jódar’s consistency has been astounding for someone who only just arrived at the top level of the sport. He has risen from No 109 to his current ranking of No 11 and he is seventh in the ATP race, a clear candidate for the ATP finals in his first full season as a professional tennis player.

After reaching his first Masters 1000 semi-final in Montreal just over a week ago, a tournament many viewers thought he would win, the madness continued in Ohio. Jódar showed his toughness in a spectacular comeback win over Denis Shapovalov in the second round, recovering from 5-1 down late at night to win. Then he laid waste the 22nd seed, Alejandro Tabilo, in round three. It took one of the best performances since his run to the French Open final from Cobolli, the seventh seed, to defeat him.

At a lanky 6ft 3in, Jódar is already one of the most devastating shot-makers on the tour, capable of generating immense pace off both wings. Like Jannik Sinner, what separates the Spaniard from the rest of the field is the fact that so much of his pace is a result of his immaculate timing.

His ability to change the direction of the ball off both wings is elite, as is his return of serve. The rest of his game, from his serve to his movement, continues to improve.

His emergence, however, has led to discussions about more than just his game. Jódar’s perceived lack of sportsmanship has been a consistent theme throughout his rise. Some took issue with his various medical timeouts in matches, including against Taylor Fritz in their Washington final this month, which have generated ample criticism.

Then there was the bizarre spectacle of his shoelaces breaking in numerous matches, leading to extended four-minute delays. His treatment of ballkids and volunteers on the court is another matter.

At Roland Garros, many even believed that Jódar had pushed a ballgirl to the side as he angrily left the court between sets in his match against Alex Michelson. It turned out to be a trick of the broadcast camera angles, with Jódar angrily gesticulating with his arms at the same time that the ballgirl stumbled back over sandbags placed on the edge of the court.

His dramatic win over Shapovalov was as remarkable due to the accompanying drama as the comeback itself, with Jódar having to pause the match on multiple occasions to change his shoelaces, to the irritation of Shapovalov. Two days later, he returned to the court with a comically large transparent bag filled with about a dozen Adidas shoes.

The notion that Jódar is deliberately breaking his shoelaces to halt his opponents’ momentum is laughable, but his impatience with ballkids and other on-court helpers, most of whom are either children or volunteers, is unimpressive.

He has already developed the entitled habit of throwing up his arms in disgust whenever a ballkid dares to hand him an ice towel or ball slightly late, a sight that always reflects badly on a player.

Jódar is clearly incredibly single-minded, aloof and not always considerate of how his actions may affect others. However, he is also only 19. As he continues his growth as a player, it will be nearly as compelling to see how his character develops.

Taxpayers to fund clear-up of illegal dumps in West Yorkshire, Surrey and Kent

The Guardian Wed, 19 Aug 2026 21:30:33 GMT

Andy Burnham promises drive to tackle toxic waste, raise fines and use AI-powered drones to detect illegal activity

Illegal dumps in West Yorkshire, Surrey and Kent will be cleared up using taxpayer money, Andy Burnham has announced, as the prime minister promises a new drive to tackle toxic waste.

Ministers have identified dumps in Bradford, Runnymede and the Isle of Sheppey, which collectively contain about 22,000 tonnes of illegal waste, to be cleared in the next phase of the government’s national clear-up effort.

Meanwhile, fines will be raised for rogue dumpers, and AI-powered drones will be used to detect illegal activity while it happens, as the government looks to prioritise prevention alongside clean-up efforts.

Burnham said in a statement: “These toxic dumps have blighted communities for too long. I said we would clean them up – and that’s exactly what we’re announcing today.”

He added: “These mountains of rubbish have been a clear sign to communities that politics hasn’t been working for them or their area. This government is going to tackle the issues that have been ignored by Westminster for too long and bring back hope.”

Hundreds of illegal waste sites have been reported across England, with a BBC investigation recently uncovering 11 “supersites” that contain more than 20,000 tonnes of rubbish.

One of the country’s most notorious sites is in Burnham’s own constituency of Makerfield, where a rotting, rat-infested mountain of waste has remained for more than 20 months. The site was identified for clean-up in March alongside two others, but locals say they have seen little improvement in the site since then.

During the byelection campaign, which Burnham won earlier this year, voters in the area told the Guardian they would vote for him specifically to get rid of that one site.

The Environment Agency says it has made 42 site visits, suspended or revoked 17 permits and launched more than 30 criminal investigations as part of its initial crackdown.

In February, Varun Datta, the ringleader of a waste crime gang, was ordered to pay £1.4m after being convicted for the organised illegal dumping of mostly municipal waste at a network of 16 sites across the country, including at a historic manor house and a nature reserve in Lancashire.

Downing Street said the three new sites identified on Wednesday had been chosen because of their scale, the risk to nearby communities, their environmental damage, and links to organised crime.

Officials said the new push to prevent illegal dumping would work better than previous approaches, in part because of new AI-powered drones which are designed to detect dumping while it happens.

The 33 drones will be fitted with light detection and ranging technology, which can create highly detailed maps of illegal waste sites.

Burnham also said he wanted police and the National Crime Agency to be given a bigger role, as he announced fines for people who dump waste illegally or fail to treat it correctly would rise from £300 to £5,000.

Tougher sanctions, including imprisonment, are already available for more serious offences.

Meanwhile, in West Yorkshire and Greater Manchester mayors and council leaders will be asked to coordinate councils, police, regulators and other enforcement agencies to ramp up crime prevention efforts.

Zuckerberg lied about concern for child safety, Meta whistleblower testifies at landmark trial

The Guardian Wed, 19 Aug 2026 21:30:11 GMT

Arturo Béjar, former Meta safety engineer, tells jury tech company was aware of products’ potential harm to children

Meta has taken a “don’t ask, don’t tell” strategy when it comes to the safety of children on its social media platforms, according to a whistleblower who testified during a landmark trial against the company on Tuesday and Wednesday.

Arturo Béjar, a former Meta safety engineer, told the jury that the company was aware of the harm its products caused children, which included its recommendations pushing content from sexual predators and violent and graphic images. He said he repeatedly raised the issue to various Facebook and Instagram executives but that they did little to resolve it.

In his testimony, Béjar said his job often included him briefing Meta’s CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, on product issues. He estimated that he spoke to the CEO at least 100 times. One email Béjar sent to Zuckerberg in 2021 showed the engineer warning of constant reports of harmful content and damage to teenage wellbeing on Facebook and Instagram. Béjar said he emailed Zuckerberg after the CEO publicly said the company doesn’t prioritize profit over safety.

“I felt that he created a false and misleading impression of Facebook’s commitment to young people,” Béjar testified.

Béjar added that he sent those reports directly to Zuckerberg because, “in my experience, when Mark makes something a priority, mountains move”.

“Did he ever respond to you?” the attorney representing the government asked.

“No,” Béjar replied. “I didn’t hear back from him.”

Béjar was the first witness called to the stand in the federal trial that started with opening statements on Tuesday. The case was brought against Meta by 29 US state attorneys general, who allege the social media company deliberately designed addictive products that lured in young people and led to them being harmed. The legal officials also claim the trillion-dollar company regularly collects data on children under the age of 13 without parental permission in violation of federal and state laws.

“I heard from many of you at jury selection that the health and wellbeing of kids is a shared responsibility,” said Megan O’Neill, deputy attorney general for California, in her opening statements. “Meta didn’t do its share.”

Other witnesses to be called include Zuckerberg and Instagram’s CEO, Adam Mosseri, along with other executives and experts on children’s mental health and addiction. Reams of Meta’s internal documents and emails have also been released as evidence. The trial, which is taking place in Oakland, California, is expected to last at least six weeks.

Meta denies all allegations in the case. Paul Schmidt, an attorney for Meta, said in his opening statements that there was “no dispute” people can struggle with social media, but that Meta had “come up with tools to try and address that”. He added the company did not allow children under the age of 13 to register for accounts on its social networks and that it had disabled more than 1m accounts of those young users.

The sweeping legal proceedings could have profound consequences for Meta. If the company is found liable, damages could be as high as $200bn – an amount equivalent to the company’s 2025 annual revenue. The lawmakers are also asking that Meta be forced to change the design of its products to make them safer for children, which could have lasting effects on the company’s business model.

During his two days on the stand, Béjar spoke about his research on harm to children as well as Meta’s reliance on advertising to make money. He said features like infinite scroll, which have been described as keeping users glued to social networks, had been a boon for Meta.

Sign up to TechScape

A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives

after newsletter promotion

“On scroll, the more views you have, the more ads you sell, the more revenue you make,” Béjar testified.

The safety engineer worked in senior positions for Meta for about eight years, in two separate stints, and has been an outspoken critic of the company’s child wellbeing practices since leaving in 2021. He has testified before a US Senate committee and has served as a witness in other social media cases that involve harm to children.

One of his motivations for first tackling the issue inside the company was seeing how his own teenage daughter was treated on Instagram. He said she received unwanted sexual advances and photos of male genitals as well as misogynistic insults. Later, she told her father that reporting these abuses through the Instagram’s established processes was either ineffective or not possible.

Béjar said that he started conducting surveys of teen’s experiences at Instagram. He found that 51% of users said “yes” to having had bad or harmful experiences within the previous seven days. Of those users, the content was taken down only 0.02% of the time, according to his testimony.

Béjar said he sent those findings to Meta’s top executives, including Zuckerberg and Mosseri.

In a quick back-and-forth, the lawyer for Meta tried to downplay Béjar’s testimony. He highlighted the engineer’s good working relationship with both the company and its leadership, asking questions like “You had the support of Mr Zuckerberg?”, “You did not leave on bad terms?” and “You’re still proud of the work you did at Meta?”

To all, Béjar answered “yes”.

‘Believe your eyes’: Masters says Premier League’s integrity cannot be doubted

The Guardian Wed, 19 Aug 2026 21:08:21 GMT

Richard Masters has sought to reassure fans that the Premier League remains “everything that it should be” after the Folarin Balogun red-card scandal called the integrity of disciplinary decisions into question.

Both Masters, the chief executive of the Premier League, and Howard Webb, the chief refereeing officer for English football, were critical of the process that led to Fifa’s ­disciplinary committee suspending the USA striker’s one-game ban for a year after an intervention by the US president, Donald Trump. Asked about the Balogun affair, Masters – who was speaking in advance of the new Premier League season beginning on Friday – said: “We should be talking about looking back on the World Cup and the football that was played, and Spain being obviously the best team and ­England’s agonising semi-final defeat,” Masters said. “We’re not. We’re talking about other issues. I think that’s a huge shame. The Balogun issue … is very difficult to comprehend, really, when you look at it.”

Masters insisted that the taint of the scandal would not reach out into the Premier League, even as refereeing conspiracy theories continue among fans. “Do people believe their eyes? I do scroll through social media every now and then. I do bump into some of the stuff that people are saying and thinking out there,” Masters said. “But I do still believe that fans, when they turn up to matches that are 99% sold out, when they watch what’s going on on the pitch, they see everything that it should be. It’s still the same.

“It’s English football. Everyone’s trying their best. Referees are trying their best. There’s lots of controversy, but it is what it says it is.”

The Premier League, as a member of the World Leagues Association, is still waiting for the outcome of a complaint made against Fifa to the European Commission two years ago over a lack of consultation over the fixture calendar.

Masters said it was vital that Infantino was properly challenged in the Fifa presidential election next year. “I think that what needs to happen now is another candidate needs to emerge within the deadline with a new offer, a different offer, that can hopefully unify the confederations,” he said.

Webb said he had been “really troubled” by the Balogun scandal, as he announced new measures to increase transparency over refereeing decisions in England. “What do we know? We know for sure that a red card was shown. I understand why it was given,” he said.

“We know that there was pressure placed by a politician on to Fifa, because that was admitted. And we know that the suspension was taken away for that particular tournament and suspended through a process which seemingly didn’t exist before the tournament started.”

He continued: “We live in a world now which is different to the one that I occupied as a referee. Decisions were previously viewed as correct or incorrect, based on your judgment. Far too often now decisions are viewed as correct or corrupt by people who want to type all over social media. They try to draw inferences around decisions that they don’t agree with and what’s the motivation behind that decision. Which is born out of no facts, no evidence.”

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

This season, English football’s senior refereeing body, now known as Pro Ref, will seek to publish the assessments of an independent key match incident panel which examines all the biggest decisions taken by Premier League referees each week. As reported by the Guardian, Pro Ref will publish some audio of conversations between referees and players during matches and will continue to use X to publish real time information during match days.

New video assistant referee specialists have been recruited at Stockley Park to expand the pool of officials as Pro Ref seeks to cut the length of time around VAR interventions and eliminate incidents where VARs intervene when – according to ProRef – they should not. “I’d rather have missed interventions than over-interventions,” Webb said. “I’d rather VAR not get involved wrongly to rectify something that wasn’t wrong in the first place, because that’s a ­damaging effect on the game.”

In a further attempt to improve the speed of decision-making, the protocol behind semi-automatic offside technology has been streamlined.

Webb said fans and players alike can also expect to see more penalty kicks awarded for holding at set pieces. “More situations will be penalised, not only in August or September, but throughout the season,” Webb said. “[But] I’m not going to commit to say we’re going to go from here to penalising lots of contact. Contact is still part of the game, we still maintain a high threshold, but this time next year, all being well, we’ll be able to reflect on a season where more offences have been penalised.”

Love You to Death review – is this all they asked the woman who faked her son’s illnesses?

The Guardian Wed, 19 Aug 2026 21:00:33 GMT

Lisa Hayden-Johnson was convicted of child cruelty, but she still insists that she didn’t do anything wrong – and barely gets a grilling about it. Her children, who speak for the first time in this documentary, deserve much more

There’s an increasingly common pattern emerging whereby documentary makers take a story that was run through the Outrage-A-Tron by the tabloids to produce headlines that warped public understanding (“Britain’s Worst/Most Evil/Most Deadly” and so on), then proceed to put back some of the lost nuance and present the more complicated original picture. Lucy Letby (“Britain’s Worst Child Killer”) has been the subject of at least two such films redressing the lost balance. Last week, the story of Rhianan Rudd (“Britain’s Youngest Terrorist”) was unpacked and its many sadder parts laid out for inspection in The Schoolgirl Terrorist?

In Love You to Death, it is the turn of Lisa Hayden-Johnson, who became known as “Britain’s Most Evil Mum” during her trial and conviction for child cruelty after years spent fabricating her son Matthew’s apparent illnesses. He was put through more than 300 medical encounters, nine general anaesthetics, four operations by the age of nine, and endured many unnecessary constraints on his life, including using a wheelchair, feeding tube and oxygen tank, until Lisa was arrested when he was nine.

Love You to Death interviews Lisa, Matthew and his older sister Laura – who has some memories of being “a trial run” for her mother’s fabrications but whose suffering is largely of the more indirect, but no less damaging, kind that comes with living in a household that revolves around an ill and disabled member, taking on caring responsibilities very young, then finding out that all of it existed only to serve another’s incomprehensible purposes.

The documentary lays out the chronology first, from Matthew’s seven-week premature birth in 2001, through his early stays in hospital as Lisa insisted he was failing to thrive because he was allergic to so many foods. It goes on through his apparently accumulating conditions, his local fame as “the boy in the buggy” whom the community rallied to help, and Lisa’s insistence to their main clinician Dr Broomhall – not interviewed, though their local GP Dr Paul Johnson is – that Matthew be referred to Great Ormond Street for more thorough investigations. This was despite Broomhall’s reluctance and the increasing suspicions among ward staff that all was not well.

Eventually Dr Stella Imong, who had many dealings with Matthew’s “quite demanding” mother on the ward and had noticed the increasing number of factors in his notes that weren’t quite tallying, confronted Dr Broomhall about the situation and the latter reported Lisa to the police. The working presumption was that Lisa was suffering from Munchausen’s syndrome by proxy (now known as fabricated or induced illness) and enjoying the attention gained by having a sick child.

It is a glaring weakness of the programme that it does not probe further into the whys and wherefores of the medical establishment’s inertia here. Especially as GP Paul Johnson all but shuffles his feet in embarrassment as he describes how confrontation “before you’re sure” can damage doctors’ reputations and hurt anyone falsely accused of harming their child. There is also mention of nurses raising concerns much earlier than any were acted upon, and any astute viewer will surely have more questions than are answered. A film about medical ethics, arrogance, cowardice and self-protection could easily work here.

But the emphasis is on Lisa and her enduring insistence – bar the occasional slight concessions – that she did nothing wrong. Matthew was ill, she says, and everything she did was to help him. The children have no contact with her now, which clearly upsets her, but there is no sign that she is willing – or perhaps able – to provide them with the acceptance of her condition and what she really did that they need to establish any kind of rapprochement. Another weakness is the lack of anything other than softball questions to Lisa. She is rarely pressed on any issue or incident and it feels like a dereliction of journalistic duty.

Laura and Matthew talk about her with regret, mystification and – particularly in Laura’s case – a longing for her to accept responsibility for their suffering. They are a study in grace and compassion. They manage to see her as mentally ill rather than “evil”, despite their experience of life lived right on the border between those two states. They undoubtedly deserve better – from their mother, from the professionals involved with their childhoods, and this programme, which – though it valuably restores much of what the tabloids eschewed – fails on some of its own quite vital terms.

Love You to Death is on Channel 4 now

The Guardian Wed, 19 Aug 2026 20:17:39 GMT

Seven people, including five Americans, were killed when a safari helicopter crashed on Wednesday morning in a remote part of northern Kenya, according to local police and the state department.

Among the dead were an executive with Telemundo, the US-based Spanish-language network owned by NBC Universal, and the director of Ecuador’s national intelligence service.

The helicopter crashed at 9.13am while flying from the Loisaba Conservancy to the Ewaso Nyiro area in Samburu county, according to the Kenya Civil Aviation Authority, which said in a statement that an investigation was under way. It said there were seven people onboard – six passengers and the pilot.

Late on Wednesday, David Nkoroi, the police commander for Samburu, told reporters that all seven people onboard had died.

In Washington, the state department said five of those killed were US citizens. “The US embassy is in touch with local authorities and is providing consular assistance,” it said. “We extend our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones on their loss.”

The identities of the victims were not revealed but a local television station in Miami, Florida, said that José Suárez, 55, president and GM of several Telemundo stations in Florida, was among those killed.

“We are heartbroken to learn the tragic news that José was killed in a helicopter accident in Kenya,” the NBC affiliate in Miami quoted from a joint statement from NBC Universal and Telemundo leadership.

The helicopter crashed in a rugged area in the foothills of Mount Ololokwe, a popular tourist destination in the country, local media reported. The helicopter, owned by local company Lady Lori Helicopters, was carrying guests with the travel company +Beyond.

Lady Lori Helicopters said in a statement that the aircraft was operating a charter flight when it crashed.

Tropic Air Kenya, a local safari operator, said in a statement that it dispatched two of its helicopters to aid search and rescue operations.

The aviation authority said the aircraft was a Eurocopter EC130 B4.

Ecuador confirmed later on Wednesday that Michele Sensi-Contugi, director of the country’s national intelligence center, died in the helicopter crash in Kenya.

In a statement posted on X, the presidency said: “In this moment of deep sorrow, the government extends its heartfelt condolences to his family, loved ones and close associates.”

Sensi-Contugi was visiting Kenya as a tourist with his wife, Stephany Hollihan Vasconez, who also died in the crash. She was a US and Ecuadorian citizen. They are survived by their two children.

Helicopter crashes have happened with increasing regularity in Kenya, which has a thriving tourism industry that depends on domestic carriers to ferry visitors to distant places like Mount Ololokwe.

In February, a legislator was among six people who died after a helicopter crash in a hilly area of western Kenya.
