Giraffe review – sparkling one-woman show stands out from the crowd

The Guardian Wed, 19 Aug 2026 19:00:30 GMT

Pleasance Courtyard, EdinburghAn unlikely relationship blossoms in Abigail Weinstock’s compelling and touching solo drama

It takes a brave writer/performer to make her character a sociopath. How to keep the audience on board with someone who is callous and indifferent?

In Abigail Weinstock’s sparkling one-woman show, 30-year-old Eliana has been caught making clandestine recordings in her neighbour’s bedroom and cannot deny it. A court summons follows. Even then, her first thought is how to game the system.

Her attempt to do so is what gives Giraffe its structure. Eliana has a fortnight until going in front of a judge who will determine whether her temporary restraining order should be made permanent. If she can drum up three letters of support in that time, she has an outside chance of avoiding homelessness (she lives too close to her victim to stay put). With no obvious advocates – her mother long dead, her stepmother intolerant and her father inscrutable – she needs extra resources of imagination to find backers.

Sociopaths, of course, can be ruthless, so Eliana is prepared to bluff her way into a childminding job (reassuring the confused mother that she wishes no harm to her daughter) and mask her true nature from a therapy group in the hope of seeming like a trustworthy citizen.

Everything goes wrong before it comes right in Emma Jude Harris’s production but, on the way, Weinstock gives a delicious portrayal of a physical and emotional misfit who is hopelessly and hilariously at sea with the business of human communication.

What emerges is a quite different diagnosis. Touchingly, in this semi-autobiographical show, Eliana understands the psychology of the silent child she looks after unlike anyone else. It proves she is an emotionally rich human being who just happens to have her own way of interpreting – and misinterpreting – the world. Standing out from the crowd in a human zoo, she and the child are giraffes among zebras. So is this show.

At Pleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 31 August

Tongue and Robinson’s high fives put England in control against Pakistan

The Guardian Wed, 19 Aug 2026 18:58:53 GMT

First Test day one: Pakistan 171; England 112-2

Root (37*) and Cox (23*) add 64 to leave deficit of 59

For all that Joe Root was playing his 167th Test match for England, and had led the side on 65 previous occasions, there will surely have been a few butterflies as he pulled on the blazer and walked out for the toss on his home ground.

Root was resuming what he once described as an “unhealthy relationship” with the captaincy, while a supposedly one-off return to the job earlier this summer ended in a crushing defeat to New Zealand. Aged 35, England’s premier batter could easily have said a polite “no thank you” when the vacancy came around again.

Yet Root appears to be driven by something more than just duty; a sense of unfinished personal business, perhaps. And if there were any nerves or second thoughts, they surely evaporated once Ollie Robinson struck with the first ball of the series to set in motion a one-sided opening day against Pakistan.

By stumps the match had progressed significantly. Robinson went on to claim his fifth five-wicket haul in Test cricket with a masterful display of wobble seam, while Josh Tongue picked up his fourth to share all 10. And in response to Pakistan’s 171 all out in 48.1 overs, England closed on 112 for two from 25, with Root 37 not out.

Plenty went for Root, it must be said, not least the coin falling his way to claim the best of conditions. The last seven Tests here have been won by the side bowling first and, while not as quick as some in recent years, the pitch was offering movement for any seamer who could lock in on the Headingley length.

Doing so is Robinson’s forte, of course. And after trapping Azan Awais lbw from around the wicket with his opening delivery – the first time a Test series in England has started with a wicket – Root’s metronome rarely missed a beat. As a result, the initial rustiness of Jofra Archer and Gus Atkinson was scarcely felt.

One of Robinson’s victims here was a touch unfortunate, with Saud Shakeel too late in reviewing an lbw shown to be going over the stumps. But figures of five for 51 from 18 overs were no less deserved, while an afternoon spell of eight overs, two for 17, was also a positive as regards his fitness and old-ball prowess.

That Pakistan did not fold entirely owed much to Abdullah Shafique, who emerged at six for two in the fifth over – Shan Masood plumb lbw to Robinson – and top-scored with 61. But for all that he looked assured, Shafique was eventually made claustrophobic by Jamie Smith’s presence up at the stumps – a notable move by Root – and then powerless as Robinson jagged one through the gate.

Imam-ul-Haq, one of four Pakistan players to have played for Yorkshire, was probably the batter left with the greatest sense of regret on the day. The left-hander had been so diligent during an initial rebuild alongside Shafique that straddled an early lunch triggered by rain and added 91 runs for the third wicket.

But after struggling with an ankle problem that required treatment on the field, Imam drove loosely to slip on 42 to hand Tongue his first wicket. Unlike Archer and Atkinson, Tongue did not look like a bowler coming off a diet of 20 balls per match in the Hundred but rather the Test thoroughbred he is fast becoming.

after newsletter promotion

So much comes down to Tongue’s natural angle that, allied with nip in either direction, can turn defence into a lottery. Here he snuffed out any chance of a fightback from the lower middle order, his figures of five for 46 seeing both the stand-in skipper, Salman Ali Agha, and Mohammad Rizwan pinned lbw.

Tongue found himself on a hat-trick after a third lbw won against Ali Usman, only for Khurram Shahzad, first-class average of 10, to lace it through the vacant covers for four. But history still came Tongue’s way as he and Robinson mopped up the last two in successive balls. Not since Steve Harmison and Monty Panesar at Old Trafford 20 years ago have an England pair claimed five apiece in a Test innings.

Pakistan (the victims on that occasion also) tried their best to muster a response. Mohammad Abbas trapped Ben Duckett in front on 15 – revenge for an umpire’s call that earlier went the opener’s way – while Mohammad Ali squared up Emilio Gay with a beauty that flew to slip to end a breezy 33 from 31 balls.

But, in a final session that ran to 7.30pm due to the earlier downpour, that was as good as it got for Pakistan. Jordan Cox contributed a confident 23 not out in his first stab at No 3 as he and Root batted through to the close. At times it was tricky to tell the two right-handers apart, which says plenty about how the rookie fared.

As much as you don’t get a second chance to make a first impression and Pakistan are clearly a struggling side, Root’s return to the captaincy full-time began as well as he could have wished for. A first win in the job since 2021 – the one amid the notorious run of one in 17 – already looks like the likeliest outcome.

An inquest into the death of a five-year-old boy who fell from a 15th-floor window has heard that more measures could have been taken to make it safer.

Aalim Ahmed, who was autistic, died when he fell from a kitchen window at a residential block in Plaistow, east London. His father, Makail Ahmed, rushed from the top floor temporary social housing flat and discovered his body shortly before 6am on 16 May 2024.

There was a long history of complaints about the council accommodation from the family, who had asked to be moved, the court heard.

East London coroner’s court heard that the Newham council property manager Nnenna Muoma thought “more restricted features could have been installed” after visiting the Ahmed family on the afternoon he died.

In a note to the council after seeing the family at Jacobs House, the property manager wrote: “Following the horrible incident and fatality, I visited the family yesterday. The kitchen window from where the child fell off is functional but can be operated by a child, hence the incident.

“There is [a] restricted feature to allow a limited opening. More restricted features could have been installed to reduce this risk.”

Muoma told the court: “That was my personal thought. I have seen other households with children with special needs with different gadgets which can be done to make it safer.”

She said she was not an expert in the area and did not know the window restrictors in place could be locked.

Makail Ahmed and Aalim’s mother, Sahra Osman, have described their son’s death as “preventable” and blamed Newham council, after claims safety concerns about the flat were reported on multiple occasions.

A postmortem examination found Aalim died from “multiple injuries due to or as a consequence of trauma” from a “fall from height”.

Osman has told the court she was “scared” and “horrified” when the council put them in the top-floor flat, which needed repairs, because her son had “no sense of danger”. She felt the property was not suitable for her young family, which also included a newborn girl, but felt obliged to take it or risk homelessness.

On the day Aalim died, Osman was sitting on a bed with her arms wrapped around herself when Muoma saw her. One of the first things Osman told her was: “I asked to be moved and nobody listened to me.”

Muoma told the court: “I said I do not have that information but I am sorry. We want to assist you and if [you] cannot stay overnight I can find you a place to stay.”

Muoma said she tried the window twice and was able to open it on the second attempt, but could not remember exactly how she did it.

The council property manager said she may have pressed a button to help open it but did not give details about the restrictor or the position of the handle. She also took a photograph of the open position to show her manager how far it could open, she told the court.

Newham council said it would be unable to comment until after the inquest concluded.

The hearing continues.

Can Andy Burnham rewire the ‘Treasury brain’ to boost growth?

The Guardian Wed, 19 Aug 2026 18:46:22 GMT

PM wants to reduce department’s stranglehold on public purse and bring long-term thinking to economic policy

Andy Burnham is far from the first prime minister to dream of taming the power of the mighty Treasury.

Boris Johnson all but forced the resignation of Sajid Javid by handpicking his team; Margaret Thatcher favoured her economic adviser Alan Walters over Nigel Lawson, prompting the latter’s furious resignation; and Tony Blair and Gordon Brown’s power struggle was the stuff of Whitehall legend.

Burnham’s approach harks further back still to Labour prime minister Harold Wilson’s Department for Economic Affairs (DEA), a short-lived attempt to bring long-term thinking to British economic policymaking.

The PM made the historical analogy as he gave fresh details this week of his plan to take control of growth policy from the Treasury and hand it to a new No 10 department in Manchester.

The DEA was responsible for drawing up a national plan for the economy, which began with the timeless exhortation: “We must pay our way in the world and produce more wealth inside this country.”

The baleful influence of the Treasury, with its stranglehold over the public finances, has long been lamented by leftwingers, who accuse it of short-term thinking and ingrained, institutional caution.

“The dual job of growth and control of the public finances sometimes clouds the growth mission,” Burnham told the Times. “Having No 10 leading on that growth mission means you’ve got maximum power to unlock the blockages where they exist in the Whitehall system.”

Some of the most criticised decisions of Keir Starmer’s tenure were seen by many Labour MPs as resulting from this “Treasury brain” – from slashing winter fuel allowance to caving in to City lobbying on a bank windfall tax.

Burnham hopes the new prime minister’s department, overseen by his powerful cabinet ally Louise Haigh, will open the space for some fresh thinking. “The new No 10 North innovation is more significant than people realise,” he said.

One of the few detailed policy publications the new cabinet has so far produced was on radical plans for devolution. The PM hopes handing additional powers to metro mayors will help bring together growth policies now scattered across Whitehall.

Ruth Curtice, director of the Resolution Foundation thinktank and a former longtime Treasury official, says coordinating across these different policy areas – housing, education, planning and so on – could be the most effective use of the new Manchester-based unit.

“No one department has all of the levers – the Treasury don’t own all of the levers,” she says. “I would see it as a positive thing that this No 10 says, ‘Given what a priority this is, we’re going to put more force behind it.’”

Former Brown adviser Michael Jacobs, emeritus professor of political economy at the University of Sheffield, draws a comparison with the Office for Climate Change, which helped to coordinate policy across government.

“The really interesting version of this to me would be a new growth unit, drawing on and made up of officials from all the relevant departments.”

Sanjay Raja, chief UK economist at Deutsche Bank, points out that Burnham’s pick for chancellor, John Healey, was instrumental in the creation of regional development agencies, way back in the Blair-Brown era.

These were meant to bring a regional dimension to growth and industrial policy – but were scrapped by the 2010 Conservative-Lib Dem coalition. George Osborne went on to create and empower city region mayors as the focus for devolution.

Given the pair’s joint interest in devolution, Raja argues that far from clipping Healey’s wings, “this is one of the more merged tag teams in No 10 and No 11 that we have seen”.

Yet not everyone is convinced that it makes sense to create a policy counterweight to the Treasury. Former Conservative chief secretary to the Treasury David Gauke says the Treasury’s control over tax and spend, which it will maintain under the shake-up, means it is inevitably powerful. “The Treasury is always going to be the most important department.”

Indeed, he suspects stripping growth out of the Treasury’s remit would just exaggerate its tendency to fixate on penny-pinching.

He also questions whether No 10 North can work: “You’re going to have this office, which will get at best a day a week of face-time with the PM, and little access to other ministers – and it will be trying to push the government in a more pro-growth direction.”

Sign up to First Edition

Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters

after newsletter promotion

A Treasury source stresses that, as the initial government announcement said, No 10 North will focus on “local growth”, and in particular devolution – rather than taking over economic strategy from No 11.

The Treasury has “lent” a small number of staff to the new unit, while its second permanent secretary, Beth Russell, who was instrumental in the creation of the Treasury’s own northern outpost, the Darlington Economic Campus, has been working closely with the Manchester team.

More civil servants are being transferred from other departments, including housing and local government, and former Times journalist Sam Lister has been appointed as No 10 North’s director. However, Whitehall veterans point to the new department’s relatively modest resources thus far.

Jonathan Portes, a former senior government economist and now professor at King’s College London, says the most important question, as Burnham’s new arrangements bed in, will be how the inevitable policy clashes will be resolved.

“What happens when No 10 wants to do something, and Treasury says no – or says, ‘yes, we’ll pay lip service to this but don’t expect any spending to go along with it’?” he says. “That has been the historic response of the Treasury when No 10 has got more powerful.”

Hannah Peaker, deputy chief executive of the New Economics Foundation thinktank, says the priority should be ensuring economic decision-makers – including the Treasury and No 10, but also the Bank of England and the Office for Budget Responsibility – work better together. “While a more devolved approach could help accelerate regional growth, the most important remedy is better coordination between economic institutions so that they are all pulling in the same direction.”

In an article for the progressive Renewal journal earlier this year, Haigh complained of the Treasury that, “faced with the dual mandate of maintaining fiscal control and supporting economic growth, the institution defaults toward caution, prioritising near-term debt dynamics over longer-term economic outcomes”.

In the run-up to Burnham’s bid for power, he appeared to suggest large-scale renationalisation of public utilities and radical tax reform would be on his agenda – alongside the long-promised shake-up of social care.

But some of these ambitious and potentially costly plans are likely to come into sharp conflict with the institutional caution Haigh identified.

With a critical budget fast approaching, the new cabinet – north and south – faces a string of decisions on tax and spend; and other key choices loom, including on how to shape the future of the beleaguered privatised water industry.

In the run-up to the last two Labour budgets, debate was dominated by the immediate challenges for fiscal policy, often played out noisily in public against a backdrop of febrile government bond markets.

Burnham clearly hopes to shape a different debate, both inside and outside government, but the historic precedent he highlighted, in the Wilson era, underlines the difficulties of reining in the Treasury.

Wilson’s temperamental secretary of state for economic affairs, George Brown, moved on after two years, by which time the national plan had been blown way off course.

His role was then downgraded so it was no longer a cabinet position and, by 1969, the experiment with a separate Department for Economic Affairs was over – and its powers had been sucked back into the Treasury.

UCL researchers warn repeated exam attempts may dent students’ confidence and raise risk of dropping out

Forcing teenagers who fail GCSEs into multiple resits has a negative impact on their mental health, according to research to be published as pupils receive their grades on Thursday.

The study by academics at University College London (UCL) compared the mental wellbeing of students in England, Wales and Northern Ireland who failed to reach a grade 4 or equivalent in maths or English GCSEs – and found that only those in England, where resits are mandatory, showed significantly lower wellbeing.

Robbie Maris, a research fellow at UCL and one of the authors, said the dent to teenagers’ self-confidence when faced with resits could be a contributing factor to the rise in young people not in education, employment or training, known as Neets.

Maris said: “Some [resitting] students will not turn up for their exams, they won’t enter them or they will drop out of education – these are the kids at highest risk of dropping out of education and becoming Neets.

“It could be leading to further disengagement, which is a worrying thing. People need to pay more attention to this, because if you demotivate or demoralise young people it puts them at risk of dropping out of the education system entirely.”

The resits policy in England was introduced in 2014 and requires students who have not achieved a grade 4 pass in English or maths GCSE at age 16 to continue to study those qualifications as a condition of their further education or college places being funded.

This year, about 180,000 students who sat GCSEs last year will retake GCSE English and about 175,000 are expected to retake maths, after record numbers of 16-year-olds last year received grades below 4.

Maris said the comparison between students with similar academic records in Wales and Northern Ireland and those in England, after adjusting for other factors, left the resits policy as a major difference between the two groups.

“We see no impact really at all for failing English and maths in Wales or Northern Ireland but in England there’s a relatively large negative impact. This is strong evidence that it’s something to do with England’s policy setting that is generating these impacts,” Maris said.

The study, to be published as a working paper by UCL’s centre for education policy and equalising opportunities, also found considerable differences between girls and boys. The biggest impact on girls was on those who narrowly missed out on a grade 4 in maths, while for boys the biggest impact was among those who were “substantially below” the threshold for a passing grade in English.

In contrast, boys who failed to get a 4 in maths, and girls who failed in English, showed little or no downturn in wellbeing.

“Girls already have low self-efficacy and anxiety in maths, on average, and we’ve got similar issues with boys doing English, anecdotally a lot of boys don’t like doing English. Being forced to resit these subjects where there are these particularly strong gender norms have large effects on boys and girls, it’s a very interesting pattern that emerges,” said Maris, adding that further research would be needed to explain why it occurred.

The mandatory resits policy for those remaining in education has been controversial since its introduction, with the success rate among 17- to 19-year-olds falling in recent years. Last year, fewer than 20% in the resitting age group received a grade 4 or above in English, while in maths about 15% got a 4 or better, and fewer than one in 100 got a grade 9.

Angela Rayner, the then shadow education secretary, said in 2018 that a Labour government would scrap compulsory resits. But the skills white paper published last year left resits in place while proposing a new “stepping stone” qualification for resitting students with grade 2 or below.

The Department for Education said: “We know that resitting exams repeatedly without improving grades can be demoralising, which is why we’re taking action to break the endless cycle of resits.

“Our new 16-19 English and maths qualifications will properly prepare students before they resit their GCSE – with changes to the accountability framework to support this and ensure students only sit an exam when they are ready to progress.

“We have also ensured that students will get at least 100 hours of teaching per subject, backed by extra funding and free teacher training, so they progress with a genuine chance of success.”

This year’s resits may see some improvement in results after the government’s toughened requirement for providers to offer a minimum of 100 teaching hours for each subject, alongside increased funding.

The Guardian view on the Ebola outbreak in the DRC: a case study in why international aid matters

The Guardian Wed, 19 Aug 2026 17:59:29 GMT

The Trump administration’s ‘America first’ approach has contributed to the scale of the crisis now unfolding in one of the world’s poorest countries

For months health experts have warned that the scale of the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) could surpass the one that swept west Africa in 2014-16. This week, the authorities in the DRC announced that a grim milestone has already been passed: at least 2,325 people have died from the virus, making it the deadliest of the country’s 17 outbreaks and the fastest-growing in history.

There is no effective vaccine against Bundibugyo – a rare strain of the virus that spread fatally undetected during the spring, often being misdiagnosed as malaria or typhoid. In contrast to neighbouring Uganda, which succeeded in eliminating an outbreak, multiple factors are combining to let the disease rip through the DRC. The worst-affected region is contested by armed groups, and a context of population displacement and chronic insecurity has made monitoring and surveillance more difficult. Ebola treatment centres have been attacked as a result of misinformation and community distrust.

The impact of this dire set of circumstances has been disastrously compounded by choices made in the west and, above all, in the United States. International aid cuts have deprived the DRC of vital human and material resources with which to fight back. In 2014, as the scale of the Ebola crisis in Liberia, Sierra Leone and Guinea became clear, Barack Obama addressed the United Nations general assembly and mobilised a global response that was crucial in containing the outbreak. The US Agency for International Development (USAID) led efforts to train local health workers, pursue contact tracing and implement an eventual vaccination programme.

The contrast with the Trump administration is stark and shaming. Last year, as the de facto head of the now defunct “department of government efficiency”, Elon Musk was given licence to implement swingeing cuts that led to the eventual dismantling of USAID. In the DRC, the direct consequence was the weakening of local health infrastructure and surveillance capacities, leaving one of the poorest countries in the world still more vulnerable. Also lost was a wealth of institutional experience and expertise gained in combating emergencies such as the one now unfolding.

The US has further undermined the capacity for coordinated international action by withdrawing from the World Health Organization, to which it had been one of the biggest donors. European countries, notably Britain, Germany and France, have also been viewing international aid as luxury expenditure and cutting back. Last year, Sir Keir Starmer announced that from 2027 UK aid would be reduced from 0.5% of GDP to 0.3%.

Against such a backdrop, the lack of diplomatic urgency over the current crisis, compared with 2014, should not perhaps come as a surprise. But that does not make it any less disappointing. The Ebola outbreak in west Africa laid bare the risk of regional and global disruption as a result of inadequate health infrastructure. A thousand pieties were then uttered in the wake of the Covid pandemic regarding the need to invest in global health security and future preparedness.

Subsequent actions by governments have belied those words, leaving the DRC exposed to an epidemic that is threatening to spiral out of control. Belatedly, the global community needs to mobilise to address the threat. More fundamentally, it needs to draw the right lessons from a case study in why international aid matters.

The Guardian view on the Grenfell Tower fire: Britain is letting companies pass the buck

The Guardian Wed, 19 Aug 2026 17:58:57 GMT

Victims received less compensation than shareholders in the company behind its flammable cladding. Parliament must make corporations pay for harm caused

There is something profoundly wrong when the company behind Grenfell Tower’s flammable cladding paid more compensation to its shareholders than to victims of the disaster. Of Arconic’s £86m in Grenfell-related settlements, all but £1.5m was covered by insurers. Hardly enough to make a multinational think again. The company whose product the inquiry found was the “primary cause” of the fire’s rapid spread has ended up paying only a fraction of the wider social cost, while the multibillion-pound bill for making hundreds of buildings safe falls largely on the state. In June 2017, 72 people – including 18 children – died in London’s Grenfell Tower fire. Almost a decade later, nobody has been criminally charged over its causes. It’s hard to conclude anything but that Britain’s system of corporate accountability is rotten.

A new report by the thinktank Common Wealth and the financial investigations group FIND suggests putting right this state of affairs in England and Wales by adopting two changes that parliament could enact quickly. The first is a “failure to prevent” law that would make companies responsible for having adequate systems to prevent foreseeable serious harm. The second is to adopt a “punitive damages” approach. Rather than compensating victims for their loss, punitive damages ask what a company should pay for its conduct. Such an award against Arconic could have been used to meet the costs of remediation, the report says, “at no public cost”.

This is possible in America. Some Grenfell families tried to bring a case under US law, where damages can punish and deter corporate wrongdoing, not just compensate victims. Currently, Meta is accused in a California court of intentionally addicting children to Facebook and Instagram in pursuit of profit. It denies wrongdoing, but says litigation potentially exposes it to $1.4tn in penalties and changes to its products. Whatever the eventual outcome, the case shows how alleged social harm can be a company-sized risk.

Arconic successfully argued that the Grenfell families’ case be heard in British courts, where civil compensation and criminal punishment are kept separate. The Metropolitan police are investigating 57 individuals and 20 organisations as criminal suspects, but no charges are expected before Grenfell’s tenth anniversary. Compare that with Hong Kong’s Wang Fuk Court fire, which killed 168 people in November 2025. Authorities immediately treated it as a potential crime involving corporate actors. Within seven months, seven people and two firms faced manslaughter charges. No one is suggesting authoritarian Hong Kong as a model. But nearly a decade without charges in Britain, against seven months in the far east, is an uncomfortable contrast.

There are reasons why justice has taken so long: the Covid pandemic disrupted the Grenfell public inquiry involving hundreds of core participants, and responsibility stretches across manufacturers, certifiers, architects, contractors and regulators. This exposes a deeper problem: the more entities involved, the easier it becomes for blame for a disaster to disappear between them.

Lawmakers know how to stop companies passing the buck. The polluter pays in environmental law. There are recall obligations in product safety and collective redress in competition law. Why aren’t legal principles that are already used to force companies to account for economic and consumer harms being extended to catastrophic social harms? Until they are, the law will remain better at protecting investors rather than the public from corporate wrongdoing.

The Guardian Wed, 19 Aug 2026 17:48:56 GMT

A father, mother and their teenage daughter who died off the Sussex coast on Tuesday have been identified.

Sussex police named the victims as Hassan El-Khawas, 55, his partner, Zeina Alayn, 37, and their 14-year-old daughter, Sara El-Khawas. A younger girl who was also part of the family is in hospital in a critical condition. She has not been named.

The Palestinian embassy in London said El-Khawas was a British man of Palestinian descent.

Police, paramedics, coastguard crews and a lifeboat attended the scene at Shoreham-by-Sea, where four people were pulled from the water.

Sussex police said the cause of the tragedy was still being investigated. It could not confirm reports that the older girl got caught in a fishing net.

The force said in a statement: “Following review of CCTV footage and initial witness accounts, the current hypothesis is that this was a tragic accident, with no third-party involvement.”

Adnan Hmidan, the chair of the Palestinian Forum in Britain, said: “According to the information available to us, the family encountered strong currents while at sea. Their daughter, Sara, became caught in a fishing net and her father attempted to help free her.

“As the waves and currents intensified, her mother, Zeina, also entered the water to try to save them, followed by their younger daughter.”

Two other children from the family were in the care of their paternal uncle, he said.

“The Khawas family are British citizens of Palestinian origin, with roots in Rashidieh refugee camp in Lebanon,” he said. “Like many Palestinian families, members of their extended family have lived in Britain for many years and have built a strong and close-knit community here.

“Our thoughts and prayers are with the entire family, particularly the children, who are facing an unimaginable loss. We ask everyone to respect their privacy and dignity at this painful time.”

Andy Burnham said the incident was “a terrible family tragedy” and a reminder of the dangers of open water swimming.

There was a huge emergency service response to the incident on Tuesday afternoon, when police were told four people had got into difficulty in the water.

Sussex police said they believed all four entered the water to swim. Ch Supt James Collis confirmed that a man, woman and a teenage girl had died at the scene.

Asked if the government needed to do more on water safety, Burnham said: “Always. It’s so sad to hear what happened yesterday, and obviously we think there’s a young girl still in the hospital fighting for her life, and we send our best wishes and love to wider friends and family. But a real tragedy, a real terrible family tragedy.”

Speaking on a visit to north-east England, Burnham added: “Obviously, we will look in detail at what happened. The thing I can say today, and there is still, I think, a further heatwave to come in this summer period, it is just to remind people about the dangers of open-water swimming. The coldness, even when it feels hot outside, it can shock people, and that can cause the difficulties. So people just need to remember that at all times.”

Two air ambulance helicopters and a critical care team were sent to the scene and Shoreham RNLI said its lifeboat had been called out at 3pm.

Burnham paid tribute to those who tried to save the family. “I do need to praise the emergency services, who I know were on scene very quickly yesterday. They’ve had a busy summer, but they were there, and we thank them. As I say, just huge sympathy to the friends and the family,” he said.

There have been a series of water-related deaths across the country in a summer of record-breaking heat. On Saturday, a 12-year-old boy drowned in the River Lea, near Hackney Marshes in north-east London.

In April, a woman and her young child died after getting into difficulty in the water in west London. Both died at the scene in Elthorne Park, Ealing, the Metropolitan police said. There have been at least 35 drowning deaths, including eight in July, according to a study by the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine.

Joss Loader, the chair of Shoreham Beach Residents’ Association, said: “There’s just a really strong sense of shock, obviously people are really concerned for the young girl. A small, tightly knit community with a very deep sense of shock and that sense of disbelief you get after a tragedy because it has come out of nowhere.”

Shoreham beach is a spit of land with water on three sides from the River Adur, the estuary and the sea, and Loader said she understood the “tragic events” had happened in the estuary.

“It’s school holidays and we have had a wonderful summer so the beaches have been packed with families,” she said. “People swim from those beaches even in the winter, generally it is considered as safe as the sea can be. You wouldn’t be swimming there and think you were taking a risk.”

Anna Peacock, 81, who lives near Kingston beach across the water from Shoreham Fort, said emergency services were on the scene very quickly.

“People come down to swim, particularly in the summertime and I don’t think they realise there’s a riptide along here,” she said. “It’s very inviting to come to the sea, but the tide could carry you out in seconds, and I don’t think people have realised that.”

All power to the UK competition watchdog’s war on ‘drip pricing’

The Guardian Wed, 19 Aug 2026 17:39:16 GMT

Competition and Markets Authority on message with PM’s planned purge of hidden fees and add-on charges

Trainline, Virgin Atlantic and Red Driving School face investigation

The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) is on-message with Andy Burnham’s declaration of war on the small – and sometimes not-so-small – hassles and expenses of everyday consumer life created by companies’ underhand and misleading pricing tactics. Trainline, Virgin Atlantic and Red Driving School found themselves under investigation on Wednesday for various forms of alleged “drip pricing” – not being upfront about mandatory add-on charges, in other words.

The prime minister had nothing to do with the CMA’s pursuit, it should be said. The watchdog’s “consumer protection drive” pre-dates his arrival and was encouraged by legislation under the last Tory government – the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act of 2024, which gave the regulator “direct enforcement” powers, meaning it no longer had to go to court under consumer protection laws. And it is using those powers: eight cases were opened last November and driving schools AA and BSM plus the ticketing site StubHub UK have already been fined.

This is very welcome. Putting a few household names in the spotlight sends a usefully strong message. By way of boosting that signal, shares in Trainline, the only quoted company on Wednesday’s list, plunged by 14%.

It’s merely an investigation at this stage, so one can’t draw conclusions, but there was a curious line in Trainline’s statement. “Trainline has proactively engaged with the CMA over several months and is taking steps to enhance the presentation of certain fees,” it said.

The obvious question is why, if the regulator has been on the warpath for months, Trainline didn’t just give it everything it wanted on day one. Regular users of the slick app know there can be a fee at the end of the booking process (for about 30% of journeys), so they are unlikely to be deterred by a message to that effect displayed prominently at the outset.

There may be complicating details. Trainline adds its value for consumers by navigating the hellishly complicated fare structures on Britain’s railways by, for example, identifying so-called “split tickets” (multiple tickets covering legs of a single journey) or cases where an obscure railcard will almost pay for itself. If Trainline’s fee depends on the type of ticket, perhaps it’s not possible to state the fee precisely until the punter has chosen.

But such dry technicalities were, presumably, mentioned in the months of engagement with the CMA. So it would be fair for Trainline shareholders to ask how this affair has even reached the stage of a formal investigation by a regulator with the power to order refunds and fine 10% of turnover. It’s not as if large sums are involved – the CMA said it observed transactions with additional fees ranging from 50p to £2.79.

Human remains again found at Lake Mead as water levels drop amid drought

The Guardian Wed, 19 Aug 2026 17:30:28 GMT

Discovery marks latest grim finding in lake as water levels in crucial reservoir outside Las Vegas continue to decline

Human remains have once again been discovered at Lake Mead outside Las Vegas, Nevada, marking the latest in a line of gruesome discoveries as water levels in the crucial reservoir continue to drop, authorities said.

These remains were discovered on 16 August, USA Today reported. The National Park Service (NPS) told the outlet there did not appear to be anything suspicious about the body.

Las Vegas police reportedly said “a non-criminal, dead body report was taken for the remains”. The local coroner said authorities were trying to identify the deceased person, as well as determine the manner and cause of death, USA Today said.

As water levels have declined in recent years, authorities have found multiple bodies. In 2022, authorities recovered a body in a barrel, USA Today noted.

Authorities reportedly said the man seemed to have been shot, potentially during the late 1970s or early 1980s. Some experts believe Lake Mead’s location near Las Vegas – an organized crime hotspot – means it’s probable still more remains will be discovered.

This week’s grim finding underscores Lake Mead’s perilously low water levels amid a historic drought and broader water crisis in the US west. Weeks ago, Lake Mead’s water level dipped to 1,040.4ft above sea level, nearing the 28 July 2022 record low.

Lake Mead is integral for water storage on the Colorado River, which provides water to about 40 million people across seven states, as well as tribal nations and Mexico. The river basin is reeling from a mix of extended drought, extreme heat, waning snowmelt and over-consumption.

The second major reservoir on the river, Lake Powell, is also seeing historic low levels as the global climate continues to warm.

“In the 21st century, the ultimate cause of the problem is declining runoff,” Jack Schmidt, director of Utah State University’s Center for Colorado River Studies, previously said of the water crisis. “There’s less water in the system. It’s caused by a warming climate, period.”

Otter spotted for first time in 100 years in New York City’s Bronx River

The Guardian Wed, 19 Aug 2026 17:27:55 GMT

Image captured in early June shows animal foraging in the waterway in first since early 1900s, signaling its recovery

An otter has been spotted in the Bronx River for the first time in more than 100 years, in a further sign that New York’s previously befouled waterways are recovering some of their ecological health.

The North American river otter was photographed by a motion-activated camera foraging near some vegetation in the Bronx River, a waterway that flows through New York’s Bronx and empties into the East River.

The image, captured in June by the camera of RJ Hawkins, a scientist affiliated with the Wildlife Conservation Society’s Bronx zoo, is the first documented sighting of a river otter in the river since the early 1900s, according to the society.

“When I first reviewed the images, I could hardly believe what I was seeing,” said Hawkins. “Knowing this may be the first documented river otter in the Bronx in generations was an incredible moment. It shows why long-term wildlife monitoring and environmental restoration efforts matter.”

River otters are found across North America and were once plentiful in New York’s rivers but vanished due to rampant water pollution, habitat loss and trapping for their fur.

The Bronx River, in particular, was treated as an open sewer and a dumping ground for New York’s rapidly expanding industrial base as the city grew into an economic powerhouse in the 19th and 20th centuries.

Factories and slaughterhouses dumped chemicals, oil and animal blood directly into the water, with untreated sewage also seeping into the waterway. The river faced the further indignity of becoming a sort of garbage tip, as people threw old tires, appliances and other unwanted materials into it.

This decimated local wildlife, but concerted conservation efforts and laws such as the Clean Water Act have in recent years helped restore the Bronx River’s fortunes, to the point that species such as oysters have returned.

In 2007, beavers returned to the river for the first time in more than 200 years, the zoo said, and the appearance of a river otter suggests the waterway, which is New York City’s only freshwater river, is continuing to recover from decades of pollution.

While the sighting of a single otter doesn’t confirm a larger resident population, it is encouraging as river otters require clean water and abundant fish.

Measuring up to 5ft in length and sporting a muscular tail that comprises 40% of their body, river otters are considered playful creatures and adept hunters. When frightened, they can emit a scream that can be heard 1.5 miles away.

“There are moments in conservation that remind us why this work matters, and this is one of them,” said Craig Piper, director of Bronx zoo.

“Thanks to a broad coalition of public and private partners, we can celebrate the return of an otter as a result of decades of restoration work to provide cleaner water and healthier habitat. It’s a win for both wildlife and people.”

Andy Burnham has said government money alone may not be enough to get rough sleepers off the streets by Christmas, as experts called for more of a plan to deal with the problems that cause homelessness.

Speaking on a visit to the north-east of England, the prime minister said he felt “very passionately” about tackling rough sleeping and wanted the wider society to play a part in wiping it out.

He acknowledged that not every rough sleeper may take the offer “for their own reasons”. But he said a nationwide effort to stop as much rough sleeping as possible by Christmas was the aim – replicating what happened in the Covid pandemic.

Burnham told reporters: “The government money may not fully get us there, and I’m saying to wider society, faith organisations, let’s see if we can do this together.

“Let’s see if Britain can do this. Give everybody an offer to come inside before Christmas. You know, that is just something we can do.

“We did it in the pandemic. We can do it again, and it’s a rallying call, really, that I’m putting out there today, with a lot of government money behind it.”

Burnham wrote in the Guardian on Tuesday that rough sleeping has become so common it now “feels like part of the scenery”, as he pledged another £100m to tackle the problem this winter.

The announcement puts tackling homelessness as a central policy for Burnham’s government, and gives voters a measure by which to judge his success.

As mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham introduced schemes such as A Bed Every Night to offer emergency accommodation, but while the number of rough sleepers fell, it then began to increase again.

He said this was because “we were the only place providing that level of support, and understandably, people then travelled to Greater Manchester to access that support”.

He added: “So my point is, we can do this, but only if all areas are pulling in the same direction, and that’s what this funding is designed to achieve – to make this a nationwide initiative as we go into the Christmas period, getting everybody behind it.”

He said people being left to sleep on the streets “can often cost more to the state because people can be in and out of A&E, and in and out of hospital beds, and sometimes in contact with the police”.

As part of the national effort, Burnham said he would host a summit this autumn to “bring together leaders from across society – from business, finance, charities, health, faith communities and more – to ask what role each of them can play in ending rough sleeping”.

Council leaders and experts have applauded Burnham’s aims but also called for more work on how to deal with issues underlying rough sleeping, from mental health problems to addiction.

Liam Robinson, leader of Liverpool city council and chair of the Local Government Association’s inclusive growth committee, said there may need to be “future conversations” about more funding to tackle homelessness, including the thousands of people living in temporary accommodation.

“It does need to be resourced more,” he said. “We know councils are spending £950m more than they were five years ago on this issue, so we’re really just talking about the tip of the iceberg with rough sleeping. There may be a requirement for more funding.”

He added that extra money may need to be for “more than just housing-related funding”.

She added that the UK needed to learn from the “temporary accommodation nightmare” to ensure the new funding was not funnelled straight into the pockets of private companies.

“I am making a commitment to donate the same of my prime minister’s salary. I’m donating part of my constituency MP salary to local organisations, but the extra bit that comes with being prime minister, I’m making the same commitment.

“I wouldn’t want to ask anybody to do anything that I’m not prepared to do. I want to lead from the front. This issue matters massively to me.”

Israel admits its soldiers fired at car in which Hind Rajab was killed

The Guardian Wed, 19 Aug 2026 17:21:14 GMT

Military orders criminal investigation into deaths of five-year-old and six family members in Gaza in 2024

The Israeli military admitted on Wednesday its troops had opened fire on a car carrying five-year-old Hind Rajab and six family members in Gaza in 2024, saying it had ordered a criminal investigation into the killing.

The killing of Hind and her family was one of the most high profile of a series of incidents involving civilian casualties during the first months of the Gaza conflict which prompted international outrage.

Hind died after a desperate three-hour phone call to the Palestinian Red Crescent on 29 January 2024 in which she pleaded for rescue. The family’s Kia Picanto car had been hit as the family sought to flee a new Israeli offensive into Gaza City. All the other passengers were also killed.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) repeatedly denied its troops had been present in the area near the incident, but investigations by media and others found evidence that strongly suggested nearby Israeli tanks were responsible.

Palestinian paramedics dispatched an ambulance to rescue Hind and stayed on the line until contact was lost, but the ambulance too came under fire, killing two medics. The bodies of the casualties were only retrieved 12 days later when Israeli troops withdrew. The IDF also admitted Wednesday that troops had fired on the ambulance.

“Following review of the findings and due to alleged failures in the coordination of the movement of the Palestine Red Crescent ambulance, it has been decided to initiate a criminal investigation of the incident by military police criminal investigation division,” the military said on Wednesday.

Criminal misconduct investigations into Israeli troops over the killing of Palestinians rarely lead to convictions.

The IDF published reviews on Wednesday into four other high-profile incidents in Gaza, saying it was launching a criminal investigation into the killing in near the southern city of Rafah of 15 Palestinian medics and humanitarian personnel in March 2025.

Troops lying in ambush for Hamas militants initially shot at an ambulance that was trying to retrieve casualties from an Israeli offensive, then fired on a series of emergency vehicles which approached their positions, according to phone footage and the sole survivor of the shootings.

The soldiers then bulldozed over the bodies and vehicles, burying them in a mass grave. UN and rescue workers were only able to reach the site a week later.

“They were killed in their uniforms. Driving their clearly marked vehicles. Wearing their gloves. On their way to save lives. This should never have happened,” said Jonathan Whittall, a UN official who helped recover the bodies.

The Israeli military initially said it had opened fire because the vehicles were “advancing suspiciously” without headlights or emergency signals. But it backtracked from that account after footage emerged showing the Red Crescent and civil defence teams driving slowly with their emergency vehicle lights flashing and logos visible.

Munther Abed, a Palestinian paramedic who was present at the incident in which 15 of his colleagues were killed, said he hoped “those who killed ⁠my colleagues, who were like family to me, face justice, real justice”. “I want to say to the whole world, ambulances 101 ​is not a target and they must be protected,” he said referring ​to the speed dial number for the Red Crescent service ​in Gaza.

The IDF said it had decided not to open a criminal investigation into the April 2024 airstrikes that hit a convoy of World Central Kitchen vehicles, killing seven humanitarian workers from the US-based aid group, which has distributed food in Gaza throughout the war.

The aid group said at the time it had coordinated with the military over the movement of its cars. The vehicles, which had the group’s logo on their roofs visible from the air, were left incinerated and mangled, indicating a series of targeted strikes.

The IDF said on Wednesday it had mistaken several individuals in the vehicles for armed Hamas military operatives, and that the convoy deviated from the previously coordinated route. But it concluded that “the decisions of the commanders did not raise reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct”. Two officers were removed from their positions at the time and three others reprimanded.

One of those killed in the strike was Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom. The Australian government has called the deaths a “tragedy and an outrage” and pressed for full accountability and “any appropriate criminal charges”. In February this year the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said he had made it clear to Israel and its president, Isaac Herzog, that there be transparency about Israel’s then-ongoing investigation into the incident. In April this year Australia’s foreign minister Penny Wong paid tribute to Frankcom on the second anniversary of her death, saying “people like Zomi are rare and their selflessness should not only be celebrated but protected”.

World Central Kitchen said it strongly disagreed with Israeli officials’ account of the airstrikes and their decision not to pursue a criminal investigation. “There has never been any excuse or justification for the attacks, and there is nothing in this account that does so. The decision is inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive,” it said in a statement.

“At the time of the lethal attacks, the IDF knew that our team in Gaza was unarmed and posing a threat to nobody. It had full visual clarity on our clearly marked humanitarian vehicles during the extended, multiple airstrikes. It knew our team’s movements, identities and activities in advance.”

The military also decided not to take criminal action over the killing of four humanitarian workers from Doctors Without Borders in two separate instances in November 2023 and February 2024. Israel later effectively barred the medical charity from operating in Gaza.

Dan Owen, a researcher at Yesh Din, an Israeli rights organisation, said that over the last decade only a tiny proportion of investigations had led to indictments while growing political pressure “further deters Israeli ⁠law-enforcement authorities from holding those responsible accountable, even when clear evidence does exist”.

A UN report published in February described “a pervasive climate of impunity” by Israel in occupied Palestine “in relation to gross violations of international human rights law and serious violations of international humanitarian law … some constituting war crimes and possibly other international crimes”.

Israeli forces say they never deliberately target civilians in Gaza and accuse Hamas of using civilians to shield its militants.

The IDF said that as part of the its obligations under international law and Israeli domestic law, it examined “exceptional incidents that occurred during combat”. “For more than a thousand days, the IDF has been conducting intensive combat across numerous fronts, carrying out a wide range of military missions in an exceptionally complex operational reality,” it said in a statement.

The war began in October 2023 when Hamas launched a surprise attack into southern Israel, killing 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and abducting 250. Israel’s ensuing offensives in Gaza have killed more than 73,000, mostly women and children, including more than 1,200 since a fragile ceasefire took effect in October.

On Wednesday, ⁠Israeli airstrikes killed ⁠seven Palestinians. Israeli military officials told local media one strike that killed six had targeted a meeting of Hamas commanders in Gaza City.

Judi Dench has inspired a new decorating trend – and I oppose it with every fibre of my being

The Guardian Wed, 19 Aug 2026 16:51:04 GMT

Reverse decluttering is here, prompting a shudder from me and my fellow neat freaks. Why would you want to be surrounded by mementos when you could be perfectly tidy?

Older doesn’t always mean wiser. Jo Whiley has spoken about a home hack she picked up from – clang! – Dame Judi Dench, and I’m afraid I’m opposed to it with every fibre of my being. Whiley is in a new phase – her four children are grownup – so she recently began the most satisfying project of all: a decluttering spree. Hard even to type those words without a shiver of anticipation. Trigger warning for fellow neat freaks, though: this anecdote does not end well.

Whiley went to interview Dench for her RHS Roots podcast and found the actor’s house “packed with family photographs, children’s drawings and memories everywhere”. Mind-blowingly, she means this as a positive. “Seeing Judi’s reminded me that lived-in spaces are often the most beautiful because they reflect a lifetime of love, family and shared experiences,” she says. “I suddenly thought: ‘Why am I putting all these things away?’” As soon as I got home, I immediately put all the family photographs back out.” TLDR: I cleaned up and then I made it all messy again. Shudder.

This sorry tale could be viewed as a recluttering, but instead it’s called reverse decluttering – and it’s a trend. Give me strength. It’s backed up by a review article from Current Opinion in Psychology, which determined that – duh – some objects help to bring significant memories to mind. Another study found that possessions could evoke pride. What, more pride than tidiness? Nothing matters more than that. Decluttering is the heroin of housework – in its addictiveness, that is. In every other way, it’s the opposite of heroin – it will make your life better and you’ll never be sorry you tried it. I live to declutter. It cleanses not only your environment, but also your mind, body and soul. I’m prepared to keep a capsule collection of essential items – everything else is to be chucked out, sometimes while someone is still using it, if they pause for long enough. I’m like a snake, constantly shedding skin and donating it to the charity shop.

Because fate has a sense of humour, I accidentally married a hoarder. The following sounds like hyperbole, but it’s completely true to say the man has never thrown anything away. If at any point since birth he was given or bought it, he still has it. He has every laptop he’s ever owned, even though all but the one he uses no longer work, which is why he begrudgingly replaced them. He has clothes from his schooldays, including a T-shirt that hasn’t fitted him for decades and resembles a cobweb because of the ratio of hole to material. If a member of his family ever touched it – even an individual he never met, even if it is ugly, broken, useless or all three – he intends to take it to his grave.

He has a mustard cravat that also smells like mustard, despite many spins in the washing machine, which belonged to a great-great-aunt’s husband’s brother. You’d be amazed how few occasions call for a cravat, unless you assumed it was none at all. My husband is like a bird refusing to budge from its nest because it’s fiercely protecting eggs, but instead of eggs it’s nonfunctional laptops, antique T-shirts and a pungent cravat.

Clearly, snakes and birds are not natural bedfellows, which is why our relationship is an endless argument about whether his items have been innocently mislaid (by him) or secretly disposed of (by me). If he hears about reverse decluttering, it’s all over for me. To continue the snake metaphor too far, I won’t have a leg to stand on. We recently had a lengthy, passionate debate over a stone; I won only on a technicality (he couldn’t name the beach it was from before the buzzer went). The route out of our house is a one-way street and there’s a no-returns policy. If he even tries to mess with the system, I’ll unhinge my jaw and swallow him whole.

Polly Hudson is a freelance writer

Food security is an issue we can no longer ignore

The Guardian Wed, 19 Aug 2026 16:46:39 GMT

Local community food-growing could be best line of defence, writes Dan Farag, while David E Alexander says the government must be more open about its emergency planning, and Antony So says we need to look beyond stockpiling food

George Monbiot is right that Britain has become dangerously complacent about food security (Britain’s scorched fields mean a food crisis – and the government is ignoring the one measure that would help, 13 August). A country facing climate shocks, disrupted trade routes and increasingly volatile harvests – all of which contribute to not only the availability of food but its increased cost – cannot rely indefinitely on just-in-time supply chains and supermarket logistics.

But strategic food reserves are only part of the answer. The other underused resource is our communities themselves. Research has shown that during floods, infrastructure failures and other emergencies, local groups, charities and neighbours are often the real first responders, stepping in long before formal systems can fully mobilise. Resilience is not just about what sits in a warehouse; it is about the strength of local networks, trusted relationships and the capacity of people to act together.

That is why food security should also be seen as a question of land use and reciprocal trust. Councils, NHS bodies, universities and other public institutions hold significant areas of underused land that could support community food-growing, local skills and stronger neighbourhood connections. Brilliant organisations such as Incredible Edible have proved this model can – and does – work. This land can and should become civic infrastructure for food, nature and belonging.

The lesson of recent crises is not limited to questions about government stockpiling of food; it should also be about investing in building the long-term sustainable community capacity that helps people withstand shocks together. Dan FaragDirector of innovation and practice, The Young Foundation

George Monbiot accuses the British government of complacency over national food security. By coincidence, on the day his article appeared, the UN publicised the recently released 86-page report Roadmap for Resilience: A UK Food Plan for 2050 by UK Research and Innovation.

This detailed document provides foresight-based assessments of the national food situation and offers a palette of solutions to the problem of food security, supported by a significant amount of research. Interestingly, it does not mention stockpiling, Monbiot’s suggested solution. Hence there seems to be a divergence of opinions on strategy.

Government bodies in the UK have been working on food security issues for decades. The silence of elected representatives is enigmatic because we don’t know whether they have shelved the problem or simply left it to civil servants and researchers to deal with. A more open debate, led by politicians, would help us assess whether the Food Plan for 2050 is wishful thinking or the answer to the problem, and whether stockpiling of food is likely to be any use. David E AlexanderEmeritus professor of emergency planning and management, UCL

George Monbiot is right that Britain needs to take food security much more seriously, but stockpiling should be understood as part of a wider resilience strategy.

Switzerland offers a useful example. Its national economic supply system requires the private sector to maintain stocks of essential foodstuffs, amounting to several months’ supply. Crucially, it also provides for stocks of agricultural inputs, including fertilisers. This recognises that if a crisis extends from weeks into whole growing seasons, national food security depends on being able to produce the next harvest.

However, stockpiles can only go so far. A government can pre-emptively fill silos with grain and still watch its population go hungry if electricity grids collapse or fuel supplies are severed. Food security ultimately depends on the complex web of energy, transport, water, communications and other infrastructure.

Britain should therefore ask not simply how much food we should stockpile, but what capabilities we need to preserve to keep people fed when the next crisis lasts longer than expected. Antony SoContributor, Just in Case: Narrowing the Civil Food Resilience Gap, National Preparedness Commission

Screens can play a key role in the classroom

The Guardian Wed, 19 Aug 2026 16:46:34 GMT

Dismissing screen use entirely fails to recognise the crucial role modern technology plays in equity, accessibility and basic school operations, says Charlotte Bleakley

Your article buries the real story beneath the headline (‘Our children are less cognitively capable,’ says neuroscientist who wants to cut screen use in schools, 16 August). Even Jared Cooney Horvath’s own data, cited mid-article, shows that moderate school device use is associated with better outcomes than no device use at all – it is only the heaviest use daily that drags results down. That is a case for sensible integration, not blanket alarm.

The article’s most significant omission is what technology means for students with special educational needs and disabilities (Send), and for those learning English as an additional language.

With continual cuts to Send funding and learning-support staff, a single teacher cannot differentiate instruction for 30 children unaided. Assistive technology – text to speech, translation tools, audio versions of lesson content – is often the only thing that allows these students genuine access to the national curriculum.

Technology in moderation is an invaluable tool, but it shouldn’t replace meaningful human interaction in the classroom. However, dismissing screen use entirely fails to recognise the crucial role that modern technology plays in equity, accessibility and basic school operations.

When used thoughtfully and purposefully, moderate educational technology does not diminish learning, it democratises it. Charlotte BleakleyTeacher, Roding Valley high school, and digital lead at Chelmsford Learning Partnership

Stop putting women through brutal hysteroscopies without pain relief

The Guardian Wed, 19 Aug 2026 16:46:30 GMT

The medical system is biased against women, says Carole Kendall, pointing to the very different way men who have colonoscopies are treated

I fully endorse everything Anna Moore writes in her excellent article on the lack of pain relief for hysteroscopies (‘It was barbaric. I was crying my eyes out’: why are so many women left in agony by routine womb examinations?, 16 August).

I have had three of these barbaric procedures, two of them being associated with being on hormone replacement therapy (HRT). All three were administered with very basic pain relief, ie a small amount of local anaesthetic, which I would compare to numbing a gum with a piece of ice and then proceeding with root canal treatment. I was offered a general anaesthetic on the third occasion, but this is way too much. At no point was anything else offered, like it is for colonoscopies.

I feel the system is biased against women. The hysteroscopies were much worse than childbirth for me – it was zero dilation to full dilation in no time at all. As a result of my three awful experiences, I came off HRT, because I have no wish to experience this ever again.

In the 21st century, the NHS should be offering women a bit more than a paracetamol and the equivalent of a bit of ice. A bit of dignity would also help – a recovery space perhaps? Or even treat us like men who have colonoscopies. Carole KendallLetchworth, Hertfordshire

‘I love provocative stories’: producer Christine Vachon on fighting for her ‘offensive’ movies

The Guardian Wed, 19 Aug 2026 16:45:35 GMT

The maker of indie classics Kids, Swoon and Poison on daring to have a temper in the 90s, what some producer credits mean – and what happened between her and Joaquin Phoenix

Trailblazing producer Christine Vachon bestrides the world of US independent film-making like a colossus. She has championed idiosyncratic American cinema for more than 35 years, scoring hits such as the romcom Materialists, which starred three superhero actors (Dakota Johnson, Pedro Pascal, Chris Evans) and grossed $108m, alongside curiosities such as Zola, a strippers’ road-trip comedy based on a string of viral tweets.

Vachon got her start in the early 1990s. Her often scandalous movies – from Poison (gay prison sex) and Swoon (gay child killers) to Happiness (paedophile dad) and Kids (delinquent teens) – dominated the cultural conversation decades before boutique studio A24 had sold its first tote bag. Her production outfit Killer Films, which she founded in 1995 with Pamela Koffler, has as its logo a cartoon bunny with a target for a body, mischievously evoking the company’s blend of irreverence and danger. “I don’t think we’ve ever made a movie that somebody hasn’t been offended by,” Vachon said in 2000.

Times change. Back then, Killer was on the brink of respectability thanks to Boys Don’t Cry, for which Hilary Swank won an Oscar for playing the murdered transgender man Brandon Teena. In 2024, Materialists director Celine Song’s gorgeous but conspicuously uncontroversial debut Past Lives became the first Killer film to receive a best picture Oscar nomination.

It has been a while, then, since Killer was the industry’s scrappy outsider. “I sometimes say we’re the adults in the room,” Vachon tells me. Now 63, the tousle-haired, New York-based producer is speaking from a terrace overlooking the sea in Trouville-sur-Mer. She is visiting family here before heading to the Edinburgh film festival for the world premiere of Killer’s latest production, Pretty Babies. Written and directed by newcomer Tyler-Marie Evans, it follows two aspiring teenage actors who run off to Los Angeles, seduced by the glamour of old Hollywood, only to slide into sex work. It is rather as if Thelma and Louise’s road trip had taken them to David Lynch’s Mulholland Drive.

What makes Pretty Babies a Killer film? “We love to encourage stories that feel personal and provocative and have something to say,” says Vachon. “It was not as if Tyler’s script was utterly original in terms of the issues she was dealing with. But she approached them in an original way. She has a real point of view and she can speak about her work very well.” She can indeed: at a recent screening, Evans explained that she intends the movie “to show that sexually objectified young women ask themselves the same questions as Dostoevsky”.

It is a confident, eye-catching debut but the likelihood of a controversy equal to Kids, which had viewers clutching their pearls at the sight of skateboarders having unprotected sex, appears slim. Would a new Kids have that effect now? “If you made the 2026 version, it probably would be shocking,” Vachon says. “Or you might say: All you’ve got to do is go on TikTok.”

Pretty Babies fits the template by heralding an emerging talent. “One of the things we can do with a first-time film-maker is put our weight behind a project to give assurances to the financiers,” says Vachon, who produced the feature debuts of, among others, John Cameron Mitchell (Hedwig and the Angry Inch), American Psycho director Mary Harron (I Shot Andy Warhol) and Todd Haynes (Poison), whom Vachon met at Brown University in the late 1980s.

Haynes’s debut, which interweaves three tales of transgression including a prison love story complete with graphic expectorating scene, won the grand jury prize at Sundance in 1991. That put Poison on the radar of rightwing US politicians with an axe to grind.

“The film had received a National Endowment for the Arts grant,” says Vachon. “That triggered an eruption in Congress: ‘Your tax dollars are being used to fund a movie about homosexuals spitting in each other’s mouths and touching each other’s dicks!’ Suddenly there were lines around the block to see the film. Yes, the controversy helped. But what really helped was an under-represented audience getting to see itself on screen. It taught me that if you make a movie for the right amount of money for a specific audience, and only they show up to see it, you can still make your money back.”

She has produced all Haynes’s work since then including the melodrama Far from Heaven and the forthcoming De Noche, which recently finished shooting. This drama about a volatile cop (Pascal) and a schoolteacher (Danny Ramirez) who flee 1930s LA together for Mexico has a stormy history. The project was the brainchild of its original star, Joaquin Phoenix, who brought to Haynes the idea of a gay, sexually-explicit period love story; the director then co-wrote the screenplay with Jon Raymond. Sets were built in Guadalajara, the crew assembled. Five days before shooting was due to begin in August 2024, Phoenix pulled out. Variety magazine estimated at the time that losses “could exceed seven figures”.

Did Vachon have any inkling of trouble ahead? “You know, I really didn’t,” she sighs. The reasons for Phoenix’s departure have not been made public, though an unnamed source told Variety that the actor got “cold feet”. Vachon took to social media to quell tittle-tattle: “If you are tempted to finger wag or admonish us that ‘that’s what you get for casting a straight actor’ – DON’T. This was HIS project that he brought to US.’”

She is reluctant to discuss the details today, and won’t speak on the record about whether Phoenix will receive a credit on the movie he co-created and then sabotaged. “Look, I don’t know what happened. He decided he didn’t want to do it. And, you know, I went to Guadalajara with a mop.” For a while, the film was dead in the water. “It was the passion of Todd and Pedro that allowed us to move forward.”

Sign up to Film Weekly

Take a front seat at the cinema with our weekly email filled with all the latest news and all the movie action that matters

after newsletter promotion

Business often overrules personal enmity in Hollywood. Even after Harvey Weinstein reportedly viciously insulted Haynes for refusing to partner with his company Miramax on Far from Heaven, Haynes and Vachon still teamed up with him on the kaleidoscopic Bob Dylan biopic I’m Not There and the lesbian romance Carol. So would Vachon work with Phoenix in the future? “I don’t know. That’s a difficult question to answer. I’m not sure Joaquin would want to work with me again.” She makes it sound as if she gave him hell – or will do when she sees him.

The film historian Peter Biskind has written of Vachon’s “formidable temper” and claims she “was reputed to have terrorised the British crew” of Haynes’s 1998 glam-rock odyssey Velvet Goldmine. “That is so not true!” she protests. “I was terrorised by them. A lot of the crew were old-school. We had a female director of photography, Maryse Alberti, and only now do I realise what she went through. Essentially it was: ‘We don’t want to work for this woman.’ Every day, I had to gird my loins.”

She admits she had “a bigger temper” in the 1990s. “But I didn’t mind if people thought that, because it was so hard to be a female producer. You were damned either way: if you had a temper, you were a bitch, and if you didn’t, it meant people could walk all over you. Whereas if you were a man and you showed any sign of anger, you were commended for being tough.”

Producers rarely become household names unless, like Weinstein, they are also criminals. The job can even be a source of derision, as anyone who has sat with an impatient cinema audience through interminable company logos and producer credits can attest. Pretty Babies lists three producers: Vachon, Jordan Wagner and one of its stars, Ashley Benson. No fewer than 36 other names – executive producers, associate producers and so on – clutter up the end titles.

The question of who is entitled to a credit is, says Vachon, “a source of distress and consternation and real knock-down, drag-out fights. A movie like Pretty Babies has an unproven director and a provocative subject matter. If somebody’s willing to put their money at risk, a credit tends to be what they want in exchange.”

I remind her of a line from David Mamet’s movie-business comedy State and Main: “An associate producer credit is what you give your secretary instead of a raise.” In return, Vachon signs off with another gag about the slippery, deal-making, belt-tightening line of work to which she has devoted her life. “How many producers does it take to change a lightbulb?” she asks. The answer: “Does it have to be a lightbulb?”
