My Edinburgh fringe odyssey: ‘The nudity is expressive, shocking – sometimes harrowing’

The Guardian Wed, 19 Aug 2026 16:42:59 GMT

There are 3,649 shows at the fringe this year, but how many embody its spirit of radical experimentation? I took a journey through foam, lube and gore to find out ...

Somewhere in Edinburgh, a man is drinking his own urine. Elsewhere, the story of a religious sect that commands its followers to use “butt plugs” plays out as a musical. In yet another room, a comedian sings the same song over and over for an hour.

It is shows like these that have sustained the welcomingly weird and ungovernable lore of the Edinburgh festival fringe. In recent years, though, the annual jamboree has been accused of becoming an increasingly commercially savvy entity. The radical experimentalism might just be intact, but does this now sit at the fringes of the fringe, rather than its centre?

Francesca Moody, one of the festival’s superproducers, says that putting on a show here has become increasingly expensive. When she produced Phoebe Waller-Bridge’s stage version of Fleabag in 2013, it cost about £10,000. By 2019, when she co-produced Richard Gadd’s Baby Reindeer, it cost about £40,000. Putting on a one-person show now, she says, costs her closer to £100,000. The reasons for this, which have been well reported, include soaring accommodation costs, funding cuts and rising production costs. Some have argued that this might dial down the risky spirit on which the fringe was founded. The ethos was different when the financial risks were not as high, says Moody. “It was a space for messing around and building your craft, your sense of taste. As a producer or as an artist, you’re working out what your voice is, and doing that over a number of years.”

Artists and producers may now want more out of it too: to be scouted for the big-time with a transfer to London or, the ultimate dream, a television series in the mould of Fleabag or Baby Reindeer. Some high-profile productions have lined up transfers before their shows debut at the fringe. The Australian writer-performer Hannah Reilly’s show Roleplay, about a woman who becomes a “slutfluencer” – which is also produced by Moody – already has a London transfer. As does Bigfoot Ripped My Dog In Half I Saw It, featuring a clown duo who cause chaos in their town after faking Bigfoot sightings. Elsewhere, the musical Bliss, which turns the traditional fairytale story on its head, will travel to London with the backing of the entertainment company ATG.

Moody believes the low-budget gems are still out there though. Comedian and fellow fringe veteran Rory Bremner agrees. Although he is a big name at the festival, with his latest show, Making an Impression, playing at the 1,000-seater McEwan Hall, he still likes to test out “work-in-development” material alongside new, unknown acts. “It’s an opportunity to try stuff that I’ve written in the last couple of days,” he says. These below-the-radar gigs take place in pubs or tents, sometimes containing as few as six people in the audience and often raising money for charity.

Moody thinks small-scale, risk-taking work will find a home at the fringe because people are “hungry” for it. “There is always going to be a weird, idiosyncratic little show in a back room or basement that people discover at the fringe. It’s just about finding it.”

So off I go on my very own theatrical odyssey to discover the “fringe of the fringe” and find an interactive act with a surprising degree of danger attached. Truthmachine plays out in an upstairs room of the city’s Quaker Meeting House and is produced by the Australian company Counterpilot. A maximum of 12 people at any one time sign up to a 30-minute participatory show with a lie detector test at its heart. If that exudes Jeremy Kyle vibes, it proves much more thoughtful and transgressive than the gimmick it first appears to be. We are seated before our own voting machines for a warm-up, in which people are selected at random, put under a spotlight and asked to state “yes” or “no” to questions that range from the conceptual (“has capitalism failed?”) to the icky (“have you ever touched yourself at night?”). It has an interrogatory feel, as exposing as a game of spin the bottle, but with strangers. I find myself wondering what might come next, and where the nearest exits are.

There is no time to escape because, before you can say “polygraph machine”, one of us is chosen to be strapped up to one. It is hardly coercive – the lie detector test is the basis on which we have all convened – but I still grow edgy. A young woman is chosen and begins boldly answering questions that become more intimate while her heartbeat and other biological measurements are taken, giving us the probability of her telling a lie as a percentage. “Have you ever had a sexual dream about a family member?” she is asked. I feel everyone in the room wince. Then: “Have you had a sexual experience in public?” “Did you enjoy it?” “Was it your idea?” “Did you want to get caught?” There are existential inquiries too: “Do you think you will get what you want?” “Can everyone be forgiven?”

Things have turned a shade Black Mirror, it seems. This is not so much a playful game of truth or dare as a carefully orchestrated experiment around group dynamics and exposure. What are we prepared to share? What will we hide from others? What brings up shame or social inadequacy? I am surprised by how relieved I am not to be the person strapped up to the biometric sensors, but also how much my discomfort tells me about myself.

I come out blinking into the daylight and head to Succubus, a one-woman horror show that features a trigger warning of cannibalism. A debut written and acted by burlesque performer Georgina Collins (AKA Strawberry Duvall), it was inspired partly by her experience with doctors dismissing her medical symptoms as “hormonal issues”. The play touches on medical misogyny but in dark, satirical ways, its social commentary as sharp-fanged as the female killer at its centre. Its conspicuously low-budget set design adds to its semblance of a B-movie feminist horror gore-fest, especially its props, which include a string of fake sausages representing human intestines.

Succubus is performed at the 60-seater Dexter stage at the Underbelly and is packed on the day I attend. Directed by Grainne Robson, it is not just an imaginative take on the notion of the monstrous feminine but finely crafted in its writing. Emily Ritchie and Zara Jayant, former theatre publicists, are its producers. “When we started the company, there were so many artists whose only resort was to wait for the door to open. We thought: ‘Why not build the door ourselves?’” says Jayant. Succubus was financed on a profit-share model, its £6,500 budget raised through crowdfunding, a supper-club, a horror-themed film quiz night, a burlesque cabaret night and a raffle.

The night show at Summerhall Arts is another horror, in the shape of Bunny! It is the name of Craig Manson’s drag alter ego, who emerges in a blond wig and off-the-shoulder gold dress with tufts of chest hair peeping from beneath. The self-produced show is gloriously scrappy but with a serious sting. Bunny is a struggling performer, desperate for a breakthrough after a decade of rejections and living in penury. In real life, Manson has been vocal about the state of arts funding in Scotland. In a blend of comedy and song, Bunny decides that the only way to correct the inequities is to kill off her competitors, beginning with an artistic director and graduating to famous actors and artists. It is fizzy entertainment, intelligently barbed.

So is Mother, Maiden and Crone at the Bedlam theatre, a loose modern-day adaptation of Macbeth by an Edinburgh-based drag troupe. Shakespeare is occasionally winched into a plotline involving the drama of a gay bar (a hen do for a bride called McBride), with a violent denouement on a dancefloor involving fatal quantities of foam and lube.

The show had a limited run in a hotel basement at last year’s fringe and has been financed through fundraisers. The auditorium is filled this year and I feel as if I have been let in on a thrilling local secret.

The fringe is famed for discovering student talent, namely through the Edinburgh University group Footlights, but the show I plump for is off the beaten-track of university comedy societies. Moth And Dog Are Dying to Get Out is a play with enormous ambition, selected for the National student drama festival at Curve theatre, in Leicester, this spring. It features two teenage boys navigating same-sex desire for each other under the oppressive forces of homophobia, peer pressure and strong-man masculinity. Written by full-time student Aidan Monks and inspired by the writings of the poet Peter Scalpello, it stars Dylan Swain as Dog and Ben Stuart as Moth. They are schoolboys, one of whom has been “outed” as gay with a graphic image stuck on his locker (a photo of his “spread arsehole” from Grindr). It plays out in flashbacks and forwards, the narrative jagged yet emotionally tender. It is a heart-rending play, as lo-fi as Succubus in its production values but full of promise and led by two brave performances.

There are other shows tucked away in studio spaces that encapsulate the spirit of experiment, such as Letícia Rodrigues’s autobiographical production about body size, 116 Grams: A Play to Lose Weight, which shocks with its expressive, sometimes harrowing, nudity. Thank You, F**k You and I’m Sorry (was there ever a more fringe-appropriate title?), is in the studio space at C Arts and is an intense, sung-through requiem that mourns a dead father. There is an audience of three on the night I attend but Welsh performer Jonathan Powell (also known as Jonny Forever) powers on, playing violin and guitar alongside the vocals. It is entirely self-funded and deeply personal.

The fringiest shows, I realise, are visible in plain sight if you look, and often nestling in the smaller spaces of established venues. Bunny! is in the modestly sized Anatomy lecture theatre at Summerhall. Another jewel of the festival is in an even smaller basement space in the venue, the former gents locker room at Summerhall.

QFWFQ, with Los Angeles performer Gregory Nussen, directed by Hannah Pilkes, is an enormously accomplished riff on Italo Calvino’s novel, If on a Winter’s Night a Traveller, with its own postmodern stops and starts, direct addresses and reflections on the construction of story. It is a small but exquisitely formed creature of the festival, full of experimental energy, intelligent inquiry and, most of all, an exciting mix of mischief and danger. Nussen leads one audience member to the toilet, makes phone calls and tells stories on stories. They are a natural comic but switch to a gripping dramatic tone when they begin their stories of coming out as non-binary, going to Jewish summer camp and then on a tour of the concentration camps in Poland. Nussen arrives at Zionism, the genocide in Gaza, the brutality of Israel’s government before they interrupt themselves with another layer of story, another voice, which states that this is too dangerous a story to be aired.

As the winner of the best solo show at the 2025 Hollywood Fringe, it is not exactly an Edinburgh festival fringe discovery, but it is an amazing find from a punter’s point of view, immaculately structured, surreal and labyrinthine. The invention and imagination makes me tingle. It is better than the work I’ve seen on bigger Edinburgh stages. The best of the fringe, found in this basement room, and stumbled across before noon. This is what the festival is all about.

‘Success story’ hailed as bluefin tunas caught off Yorkshire for first time since 1960s

The Guardian Wed, 19 Aug 2026 16:36:55 GMT

Researchers laud return of giant tuna to North Sea after being fished almost to point of extinction

Researchers have lauded two giant bluefin tunas being caught off the coast of Yorkshire for the first time in more than six decades as a “success story” for marine conservation.

The tunas, which were caught a day apart off the coast of Whitby earlier this week, have mostly been absent along the north-east coast of Britain since the 1960s.

While small numbers of the species have been spotted in the waters around Yorkshire in the previous years, the pair were the first to be caught for market from the North Sea since licences to catch the fish were issued in July.

Rodney Forster, a professor at the University of Hull and head of the Hull marine laboratory, called the tuna’s reappearance a “success story about the management of fisheries” in Britain.

“They were fished almost to the point of extinction in their spawning grounds in the Mediterranean through the 70s and 80s,” said Forster.

“But now careful protection of the stock means they’ve increased, even to the point that they’re now spreading back out to their old grounds around the UK and even into the Baltic Sea.”

Forster said the tuna were not the only marine life that had returned to the Yorkshire coast, pointing out that minke whales and bottlenose dolphins had seen a noticeable increase in numbers around the North Sea over the past decade.

Bryce Stewart, a senior research fellow at the Marine Biological Association, a marine charity based in Plymouth, called the return of bluefin tuna to the UK “fantastic” and lauded the work done by the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas (Iccat) to re-establish populations.

“It seemed like an era that had gone for ever, you know, I mean normally if we lose a large species like this from an area of sea, they don’t come back,” said Stewart. “So, as I said, both from a personal scientific point of view, this is a really wonderful thing to see.”

Despite joy at the tuna population increasing around Yorkshire and beyond, concerns have also been raised that their increased numbers farther north could in part be linked to the effects of climate change.

Both Forster and Stewart mentioned rising temperatures in the North Sea as another factor in the tuna’s return, albeit a less influential one than the management of fisheries.

Stewart said the warmer temperatures had a “sort of knock-on effect” as the small fish that tuna eat, such as herring and sprat, do better in warmer temperatures. Both of the fish caught in Whitby were notably well fed, with each weighing about 320kg (700lb), roughly double the size of the average tuna found on the south coast.

Climate change is one of many factors alongside pollution and illegal fishing that could prevent the tuna from properly re-establishing themselves along the Yorkshire coast, but there are hopes that if properly managed they can thrive there and even move into Scottish waters.

Calum Duncan, the principal policy specialist at the Marine Conservation Society, lauded the regeneration of the tuna populations, but warned that their continued survival hinged on consistent care and for British fishing policies to place a greater onus on protecting marine ecology.

“We’ve got a long, long way to go, but it’s really encouraging to have achieved this,” said Duncan.

“Stories like the return of bluefin tuna send a clear signal that human beings can manage our way out of environmental decline by making good decisions and working together, making good plans and – most importantly – implementing them. But we just need to do a lot more of it and need to ramp it up.”

Açaí, chipotle and gnocchi – and other words you are probably mispronouncing

The Guardian Wed, 19 Aug 2026 16:29:38 GMT

The English language can seem designed to trip us up, whether we’re greeting a colonel or travelling to Worcestershire. Here are some of the biggest stumbling blocks

Name: Açaí.

Age: First imported to western countries from South America as freeze-dried pulp in the 1990s.

Appearance: A small, dark-purple berry, or a purée made from them, commonly used in smoothies.

It has bits coming off it. Sorry?

There’s a sort of chin whisker hanging from the “c” and something weird is going on with the dot over the “i”. Those are accents, designed to help you pronounce the word correctly.

They’re no help to me. That could explain why açaí is the most mispronounced word in the UK, often rendered in speech as “ack-eye” or “ah-sigh”.

How should I be saying it? “Ah-sigh-ee”.

Seriously? Açaí is just the tip of the iceberg. It tops a new list of 20 commonly mispronounced words.

What are some others? Quinoa came fourth; gnocchi came fifth; chipotle was seventh.

Are you sure this isn’t a list of Britain’s least-ordered menu items? Not all the words on the list are foods. Segue, often mispronounced “seeg” instead of “segway”, was second. Worcestershire came sixth.

What? Knowing how to pronounce Worcestershire is the only advantage Britons have over the rest of the world. Those days are over.

Who came up with this list? It’s from a recent poll of 2,000 people commissioned by Škoda.

Why would a Czech car company care how I pronounce chipotle? I think it is trying to make a point because Škoda is often mispronounced as “scoder” rather than “shkoda”. And, obviously, it’s a publicity thing.

Does Škoda think it’s good publicity to humiliate a country? Beneath the confusion over imported foodstuffs and the never-ending debate about how to say gif, it does seem that an identity crisis is unfolding.

What do you mean? People in Britain have forgotten that some of their peculiar pronunciations make English a nightmare for foreigners.

Can you give me an example? The word colonel came 15th in the poll. Some British people think it’s pronounced as it is spelt, when it should be pronounced “kernel”, which isn’t how it is spelt.

Ludicrous. Likewise, some of those polled mistakenly pronounced “squirrel” as a single-syllable word to rhyme with “girl”, instead of a two-syllable word that doesn’t rhyme with anything.

I’m sure we can find something it rhymes with. Good luck with your search.

I have one more, slightly embarrassing question … It’s pronounced “chi-poht-lay”.

Do say: “There once was a man from Wirral/ who woke up in bed with a squirrel …”

Don’t say: “Do you have any blueberries?”

Can anyone be too poor to buy a toothbrush? Yes – I know, because that was me

The Guardian Wed, 19 Aug 2026 16:09:08 GMT

LBC’s Nick Ferrari can’t see what is stopping people buying a cheap toothbrush, but the grinding reality of living in poverty creates its own priorities

I don’t listen to Nick Ferrari on LBC very often. His antagonistic way of dealing with complex problems gets me screaming at the radio far too easily. Last month was a perfect example. Someone from the Joseph Rowntree Foundation was on discussing research showing that about 7 million people are struggling to afford basic essentials, including toothpaste and toothbrushes, because of the cost of living crisis.

This did not strike me as a controversial finding. The cost of fuel, heating, food, school, clothes – everything – has gone up, while wages and benefits have not risen enough to keep pace. Ferrari, however, latched on to the toothbrushes. I found myself listening to him talk about the price of cheap toothbrushes in pound shops and at Asda. At times, it sounded like a price-comparison advert. At other times, it sounded like lazy journalism: take a complicated issue, strip it of all context and turn it into something that will generate outrage, clicks and applause.

Had I been on the show, I would have brought both my lived experience and my academic knowledge to the argument. I would have explained why a person living in poverty might buy cheap wine instead of a cheap toothbrush.

The first thing I would have talked to Ferrari about is decision-making. How we decide what to buy, what not to buy and where to spend our money is shaped by far more than price. One of the first questions we ask, often without realising it, is whether the thing we are buying will help us now or later.

You know those people who buy 48 toilet rolls because they are on special offer? They can look ahead and think: spending more now will save me money later. Psychologists might describe this as delayed gratification. It requires the ability to resist an immediate need or reward in order to benefit in the future.

Stress makes that much harder. When people are under constant pressure, they tend to focus on the here and now. What can I fix today? What problem is shouting loudest? What can make things feel slightly better for the next few hours? A toothbrush is an investment in the future. So is going for a run. So is buying healthier food that costs more and takes longer to prepare. The benefit is delayed.

Poverty, on the other hand, creates urgent problems. The debt collector is knocking at your door for his money. The electricity is about to run out. The school is asking for payment for a trip. Your son is being bullied because he is wearing cheap trainers instead of Nikes. These things feel immediate. The possible dental problems caused by not replacing a toothbrush feel far away. That does not make the decision sensible. It makes it human.

Long-term planning becomes more difficult during periods of stress. It is also shaped by how and where you grow up. If you are raised in an environment where life feels unstable and the future feels uncertain, it can be much harder to believe that sacrificing today will bring a reward tomorrow. According to some studies, growing up poor can even affect the development of your brain – the areas associated with reward are more active than those responsible for reasonable decision-making.

That is part of the reason poverty is associated with higher levels of addiction and criminality. Not because poor people are naturally reckless or immoral, but because deprivation, stress and hopelessness shape our brains and our behaviour.

Had I been sitting opposite Ferrari, I might have asked him whether he had ever been told to change his habits. Most of us have struggled to change something about ourselves, even when we knew exactly what we were supposed to do. If making the right choice were simply a matter of knowing what was best, we would all eat the salad, go for the run, stop smoking, drink less and buy the toothbrush.

But human beings do not make decisions like machines. Our choices are influenced by stress, habit, upbringing, perceptions of self-worth, addiction, fear, exhaustion and whether we believe there is any point in planning for the future. I know this because I have made the choice not to buy toothpaste many times.

I did not do that because I was stupid or a bad person. I did it because of how I lived, how I grew up and how I felt about myself shaped what I believed was worth spending money on. My parents did not brush their teeth or ours. Looking after your teeth was not something I had been taught to value. I had such low self-worth that my own health was often the last thing on my mind.

The same was true of sanitary products. When I was living on around £35 a week benefits in the 1990s, I sometimes bought three bottles of Diamond White rather than spending 50p on tampons. You might judge me for that. But when you live in shit, when nobody seems to care about you and you have stopped caring about yourself, a few bottles can feel like an escape. It felt easier to stuff my knickers with toilet roll from the cash-in-hand job I worked and have one night away from the misery than to sit sober with the constant belief that I was failing myself and my son. At times, it felt like the choice was three bottles or dying.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

That may seem hard to understand when your life has always contained safety, options and hope. But all you have to do is ask yourself one important question – would anyone choose that type of life if they could choose another? The answer to that is simple.

I am glad I stayed alive long enough to learn that poverty is not created by the bad choices of poor people. It is created and maintained by systems that leave people without security, support or genuine options – and by powerful people who reduce those lives to lazy tropes that reinforce stereotypes about irresponsibility. You cannot call something a choice when the alternatives are not equally available.

Putting a 49p toothbrush on a supermarket shelf does not mean everyone has the money, the stability, the knowledge or the headspace to buy it. Availability is not the same as access, and access is not the same as capacity.

Of course, people should buy toothbrushes. But repeating the price of one as though it disproves poverty is not analysis. It is ignorance dressed up as common sense. Choice is far more complicated than that. I think choice is a myth for many people; it is an idea that is inflicted on poor people by people in positions of power so they don’t have to do anything to help.

Dr Katriona O’Sullivan is a psychologist, author and professor at Maynooth University. She is the author of the bestselling memoirs Poor and Hungry, and is a weekly columnist for the Irish Independent

Belgium’s De Keersmaeker was caught well before the finish and Wiebes, winner of the first two stages of the recent Tour de France Femmes, powered over the line ahead of the bunch.

The race resumes on Thursday with the second stage taking place between Clitheroe and Blackpool.

Unhinged White House response shows senator’s ‘Natalie’ barb struck a nerve

The Guardian Wed, 19 Aug 2026 15:41:19 GMT

Senator Jon Ossoff, who is up for re-election, came up with arguably the standout line of the midterm elections so far

Jon Ossoff really struck a nerve. That much is clear.

The US senator for Georgia, running for re-election in November, came up with arguably the standout line of the midterm elections campaign so far when discussing Donald Trump at a rally on Sunday.

“While the sailors on the [USS Abraham] Lincoln fight his war, while he fruitlessly drains our munitions and oil reserves, the president sleeps through his meetings. He golfs and trades stocks,” said Ossoff. “See, he doesn’t want to do the job.

“He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the Emir of Qatar.”

Not only did the remark enter into national consciousness the existence of “Natalie” – Natalie Harp, the 35-year-old aide to Trump who rarely leaves the president’s side – Ossoff’s riff also succeeded in upsetting Steven Cheung, Trump’s director of communications.

“Jon Jackoff,” Cheung wrote on X on Monday, misspelling, perhaps deliberately, the name “Ossoff”, “has to be the biggest cuck loser in politics. Instead of denigrating hard working people serving their country, Jon should look deep into his soul and ask himself why he’s a miserable person who hates this country. It’s because he’s a radical, extremist Dumocrat.”

Even for someone in Trump’s orbit, where outbursts against political opponents are commonplace, this plumbed new lows. What could possibly have triggered Trump’s stoutly built, middle-aged communications guru into attacking Ossoff, the handsome, athletic, 39-year-old senator?

It’s hard to be sure. But, apropos of nothing, this essay by Dana Schwartz, from 2016, examined why rightwing men are obsessed with calling people “cucks”:

“‘Cuck’ is a concept borne [sic] out of insecurity: a fear that one is inadequate, sexually or otherwise, and that inadequacy will lead to the loss of the things that are important to him,” Schwartz wrote.

In any case, Trump wasn’t far behind Cheung, calling Ossoff a “Pee-wee Herman lookalike” – a reference to a TV and film character whose popularity peaked 40 years ago. (Trump has also called Ossoff “Pinky Herman”, which is neither a character nor a thing.)

The anonymous White House Rapid Response X account joined in too, branding a CNN reporter who had asked Trump about Ossoff a “disgraceful, humiliating embarrassment to her alleged profession”, and later posting:

“Someday, your children will come across your disgusting and inhumane question. They will be sickened and embarrassed to have a parent be so callous and vindictive. It’s quite troubling.”

It’s hard to really be shocked by any of this any more, with daily attacks on the media from the president and his most senior aides, but an official White House account, with 2.2 million followers, invoking a reporter’s children prompted widespread criticism.

A deep dive into the policies, controversies and oddities surrounding the Trump administration

after newsletter promotion

In truth the rhetoric from Trump and his acolytes, always bellicose, has been getting worse for a while – and people who dare to publicly question Trump’s narrative that he is a successful, popular president, seem to particularly trigger those on the right.

Take James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for US Senate in Texas, who is running neck and neck against Ken Paxton, whom Trump picked for the Republican side.

Talarico’s popularity in a traditionally red state has seen Republicans come out swinging. Trump dubbed the Democrat “Talafreako” in July; earlier US senator Bernie Moreno had called Talarico, “a far left freak”, while a Texas congressman falsely claiming Talarico “daydreams about trans kids”. (There was also Trump branding a reporter “piggy” after she asked him a question onboard Air Force One.)

Perhaps the fury is prompted whenever something, or someone, succeeds in puncturing the alternate reality that Republicans have created for themselves: a reality where the GOP is not predicted to suffer heavy losses in November’s midterms, and one where Trump is a spry, capable president.

When someone points out that Trump is an 80-year-old, easily distracted man who is overseeing an ill-defined, meandering war in Iran, while doing little as prices soar at home, it appears to bring out the particularly vulgar insults. Ossoff did all this on Sunday – and sparked fresh speculation about the president’s relationship with a close aide.

With Karoline Leavitt, the White House press secretary, stepping down, there is some jostling taking place in Trump’s circle to replace her, perhaps explaining the amped up language as each potential successor seeks to be more pugnacious than the last.

And given Democrats in Congress will be running on Trump’s unpopularity this November, there’ll be plenty of opportunity for bellicose responses from the White House. We should brace ourselves for plenty more of this sort of thing.

Reform politicians are such a joke, they deserve a slot on the Edinburgh fringe

The Guardian Wed, 19 Aug 2026 15:28:33 GMT

Nige’s gift, Dicky’s love of global heating and so much more – what fun it is watching the party implode

You would need to have a heart of stone not to fall about laughing. There was a time not so long ago when Reform could give a passable impression of a vaguely functional political party. One that knew its audience and had learned how to get its message across through the media. Admittedly this was largely because the party was a one-man band with all its MPs accepting that they owed their entire existence to Nige. They were satellites to his sun. Nigel Farage was Reform, and Reform was Nige.

In recent months, though, things have been falling apart and Reform now resembles an anarchic end-of-the-pier clown show. And chaos has seldom been this entertaining. The fun started when Nige had an uncharacteristic fit of humility and tried to pretend he was only a first among equals with the grandiose announcement of a “shadow cabinet” of four people. Largely because that’s about as many serious politicians as he had at his disposal.

The trouble with this was the country took one look at Robert Jenrick, Suella Braverman, Richard Tice and Zia Yusuf and thought it must be a joke. Was that really it? The idea of any of them in charge of a government department was genuinely terrifying. And Zia can’t even get elected as an MP. It’s doubtful any Reform constituency association wants anything to do with him. He’s a man whom people dislike on sight – it saves time that way – and who appeared to have been admitted to the Reform elite only because he had a lot of money that he was prepared to give to the party.

That was just the start, though. Then came the money troubles. The £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne that Nige has never satisfactorily managed to explain. Other than as the going rate for a lifestyle most of his Clacton constituents could only dream of. There were also the financial transactions that originated from Posh George and his mum that were deemed worthy of investigation for money laundering. Hardly the stuff of the man of the people. As for Nige’s decision to call a diversionary byelection, that too has backfired spectacularly. Beating a man with a bin on his head was hardly sticking it to the establishment.

With Nige having taken to lying low, Reform appears to be in freefall. Its latest circus act has been to suspend one of its most prominent members, Tim Montgomerie, and for the row to become public. Montgomerie was about as loyal to Reform as someone who defected from the Tories a while ago could be. Which is to say, he was as close to being a loyalist as you can get. He actually believes in what the party is doing, rather than using it for career advancement.

Though, for a bright man, Tim has been extraordinarily dim. He thought that when Nige had told him he wanted intelligent voices to challenge his ideas, he had actually meant it. Forgetting that Nige is a narcissist through and through who can’t tolerate a word of criticism. When Nige says he wants to test his ideas, what he actually has in mind is a few emails from Tim telling him how marvellous he is. As Dicky Tice will tell you, the only safe place with Nige is when your head is firmly implanted in his bum.

Even so, Tim might have survived if he had contented himself with just sending a few unwanted messages to Nige. But Tim is a believer who can’t keep quiet. He’s a top rent-a-gob on the rent-a-gob media merry-go-round. Seldom off the radio or TV. So Tim made no effort to hide his dissatisfaction with Zia. In particular, he didn’t like the way Zia appeared to be enjoying himself when he was announcing ever more extreme ways to control immigration. It wasn’t that Tim didn’t believe in the policies. He just thought Reform should appear to adopt them with a heavy heart.

This was a bad category error. Tim should have realised that taking pleasure in being unpleasant to foreigners is central to Reform’s appeal. When Zia suggests he wouldn’t mind firing shots into the small boats or starting a war with France, he is only saying what other members of Reform are thinking. The word made flesh. Reform isn’t about Making Britain Great Again. It’s about bringing the fun back into politics. Making the profane sacred.

But this wasn’t even Tim’s biggest mistake. That was to imagine he was allowed to utter a word of criticism, no matter how helpfully intended. The rules on this are strict. Only Nige is allowed to fall out with other members of the Reform inner circle. He makes the rules as he goes along. What’s acceptable one day may not be so the next. So it’s quite possible that Nige is equally fed up with Zia but isn’t ready to do anything about it. Tim should have learned to keep his mouth shut. And he has found himself learning the hard way.

In the meantime, Zia has been rushing on his run. Perhaps realising that his time in Reform may be limited and determined to take the party down with him. Not caring whom he offends in his efforts to settle a few scores. Just the other day he posted on X that those MPs with the title “right honourable” were generally the most dishonourable people he knew. Now, you might think that was a dig at some Labour and Tory privy councillors, but it can’t have escaped his attention that two of them are Honest Bob and Suella. He is starting his own civil war.

And it’s catching on. Albeit in Dicky’s case almost certainly by accident. Because Nige’s silence has allowed Dicky to imagine he has a mind of his own. Which, of course, he doesn’t. So that’s why he has been holding press conferences in which he has been happy to embarrass himself and make Reform look stupid. For instance, by appearing to welcome the climate crisis, with the suggestion we should all be taking advantage of the drought by embracing food insecurity and increased deaths among the over-60s.

But in an otherwise quiet August, they are doing us a favour with some of the best entertainment on offer. Next year they should try the Edinburgh fringe.

Reform says we need to choose between climate and economy. It’s wrong

The Guardian Wed, 19 Aug 2026 15:10:12 GMT

The party’s deputy leader Richard Tice says we should stop worrying about extreme heat and enjoy it. This dangerous nonsense will wreck our finances and the planet

So now we know: the smart response to the UK’s summer of record temperatures is to do precisely nothing. According to Richard Tice, Reform UK’s deputy leader, the climate crisis is just one of those things. Nothing can be done about it, so we should simply bask in the sunshine.

It is reasonable to assume Tice would not have said anything quite as crass had he been addressing people in Stourbridge who have seen their homes burn to the ground. Or the farmers whose crops shrivel in parched fields. Or the firefighters exhausted from battling wildfires across Britain.

Yet Tice clearly thinks he is on to something. The cost of living crisis has put the government’s commitment to achieving net zero by 2050 under the spotlight. The assumption underlying Tice’s comments is that there is a trade-off between tackling the climate emergency and raising, or even maintaining, living standards – and that for the time being, the latter should take priority.

The government has certainly been acting as if it believes this is the case. While the drought affecting most of England and Wales makes the strongest possible case for hastening the green transition, Andy Burnham’s focus has been on reducing prices for consumers, including by cutting VAT on electricity bills.

It took the prime minister an awfully long time to use the words “climate change” to explain this summer’s heatwaves. He did so only after the devastating fires in Stourbridge and when prodded by a letter from green groups calling on him to end his silence.

At one level, the emphasis on putting cash in people’s pockets makes sense. Traditionally, interest in the environment waxes during periods of strong economic growth and wanes when times are tough. Climate breakdown slips down the list of priorities for voters when they are worried about losing their jobs or struggling to pay their bills. Peaks in concern have tended to come at the end of long booms, such as the early 1970s or the late 1980s.

But opinions are changing across the political spectrum. As the Conservative peer David Willetts has pointed out, 86% of Britons see climate breakdown as at least partly responsible for the recent heatwaves, and even 63% of net zero opponents make that connection. More than a third of Reform UK voters said tackling climate breakdown should be more of a priority in a recent poll.

There are good reasons for the high level of public concern. The rate of food price inflation has also been coming down in recent months, but a poor harvest means that trend could well go into reverse soon.

Meanwhile, a report by the German insurance company Allianz has exploded the myth that governments have a choice between growth and the environment. The study shows that extreme heat poses structural challenges to many rich countries because, as temperatures rise above 30C, workers struggle to do their jobs and their productivity suffers. The higher the thermometer rises, the greater the losses.

For the most exposed countries – especially those in continental Europe – the hit to economic activity will be considerable: over a five-year period the impact of extreme heat could knock a cumulative 5-7% off GDP.

According to Allianz, the UK has hitherto been below the 30C threshold and has not been one of the countries at risk from extreme heat. But on the basis of this summer, Britain may soon become a higher-risk country alongside France and Spain.

To be sure, Britain is responsible for only a small fraction of the world’s CO2 emissions, and there is a legitimate debate about how to achieve net zero. But the warning signs are flashing red. Now is not the time to go slow on tackling climate breakdown. The longer that action – global as well as domestic – is delayed, the greater the risk that the climate crisis will eventually wreck the economy.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

A failure to invest in basic infrastructure needs to be remedied fast. People faced with hosepipe bans have the right to ask why Britain has not built a reservoir in 30 years. The electricity grid was designed and built for fossil fuels rather than renewables, and many green projects are held up by a lack of capacity.

The UK’s housing stock is woefully inefficient. Household bills would be lower if existing homes were retrofitted with insulation. New homes should be subject to tougher building regulations to make mechanical ventilation – which keeps temperatures stable year-round – mandatory.

None of this comes cheap. The state will have to invest in new infrastructure as well as making changes to the planning laws. Subsidies will be required to provide incentives for consumers to go green. No question, there are costs involved in the net zero transition, but they are outweighed by the benefits. These include cheaper running costs for electric vehicles and lower energy bills for homes where gas boilers are replaced by heat pumps.

Governments can always find the money when the occasion dictates. When the security of the nation is at risk, ways to finance extra spending are found. To take one example, ministers have committed to raising defence spending to 3.5% of GDP by 2035 because of the perceived threat from Russia.

But which is the greater threat? Is it Russia, bogged down in Ukraine after more than four years of attritional fighting, or is it the climate crisis? The answer should be obvious.

Larry Elliott is a Guardian columnist

‘We never apologised for our rage or revenge-seeking’: riot grrrl legends Heavens to Betsy reunite

The Guardian Wed, 19 Aug 2026 15:00:16 GMT

Alongside Bikini Kill and Bratmobile, Corin Tucker and Tracy Sawyer created a feminist punk vernacular that’s still inspiring the likes of Olivia Rodrigo. They recall the clarity and conviction of their historic teenage exploits

Back in June, a cut-and-paste photocopied flyer began appearing on telegraph poles around Portland, Oregon, promoting a DIY show by an apparently defunct band at an intimate community space. The band hadn’t mentioned it online, but hopeful fans bought every ticket anyway. Their bet paid off: the gig really was the first in 32 years for Heavens to Betsy, the pioneering feminist punk duo of drummer Tracy Sawyer and singer-guitarist Corin Tucker – the latter’s band before Sleater-Kinney unleashed her visceral vibrato unto the world. Tucker proudly made the flyer herself.

Heavens to Betsy were barely out of high school when they played their very first show, 35 years ago this week, in Olympia, Washington, a two-song set as part of a now-mythical indie fest dubbed the International Pop Underground Convention. The festival also featured the likes of Fugazi, Bikini Kill and Melvins; meanwhile Heavens to Betsy had practised only a couple times. Before an audience of about 100, Sawyer was so terrified that all she could think was, “This has to be over soon.”

This summer’s gig was less frightening, looking out on kids the same age that Tucker and Sawyer were when they started the band. “They were singing along to a lot of the songs,” Tucker, now 53, says on a video call from her home in Portland. “They knew all the words and were screaming them at the top of their lungs.” After the gig, Sawyer, 52, recalls from her yard in Oakland, California, “20-year-old kids came up to me and said, ‘I’m learning to play drums by listening to Heavens to Betsy records.’”

Those early-90s feminist-revenge songs – about body image, sexual abuse, abortion, periods, worker exploitation, defying a world that conditions women to be small – will underpin the band’s upcoming tour of the US, as well as Baby’s Gone, a new LP collecting a 1992 rare demo tape and two 7in EPs. That inventive eight-song demo was recorded by Molly Neuman of Bratmobile with a four-track she checked out of the media library from Evergreen State College in Olympia, and only circulated on around 100 cassettes dubbed by the band.

Active from 1991 to 1994, Heavens to Betsy released one album, Calculated, and rounded out riot grrrl’s OG trifecta alongside Bikini Kill and Bratmobile (who have both reunited in recent years to rapturous crowds). Turning their spare setup into an extreme sound, Heavens to Betsy made songs that were emotional, fearsome and dead serious. “I will decide my life / No man is gonna rule my life,” they declared on Decide.

Riot grrrl records and zines – which, in Tucker’s words, put academic feminist ideas into a teen-girl vernacular – have struck a chord with every subsequent generation, echoing through the DIY underground on to the 2010s defined by Tavi Gevinson’s Rookie magazine. Olivia Rodrigo claims it as an influence; Bikini Kill will play her women-led Daisy Chain Fields festival in California this month. But the enduring power of this incendiary music has always been how its rawness leaves the door open, telling fans that they could do this, too.

Heavens to Betsy were originally signed to Kill Rock Stars. Last autumn, the label approached Tucker and Sawyer about a long-overdue wide release for the demo. “The whole thing felt like an impossible dream,” Tucker says. “I thought I had lost the physical master a long time ago.” But the label was able to make a new master from the cassette, and as they emailed back and forth, they slyly floated another idea: “And you guys could do a show, maybe?”

“I think both of us were like, I don’t know!” Tucker laughs nervously.

The duo had only kept in touch “a little bit”, Sawyer says, in the decades since their breakup; both are mothers of two. “I was apprehensive about the thought of playing these songs from when we were so young,” Sawyer admits. “Playing them now in our 50s felt daunting, like, does that even make sense? A whole lifetime has passed. But the more we talked, and the more I started listening to the songs again, it absolutely made sense.”

Tucker hadn’t listened to some of those spartan demo recordings since the tape came out. “There’s a really particular voice with Heavens to Betsy, a way of writing a song that speaks to the clarity you have as a young person: This is wrong. This is not OK. I felt really energised and empowered by that voice coming back into my life,” she says. That invigorating clarity pierces Heavens to Betsy songs in bloodcurdling, teen-girl screams – which, Tucker concedes, she could not realistically pull off in 2026 and make it through a whole show. But she hopes her conviction will communicate that anger. “It’s really important to me that that comes across in a way that’s absolutely not softened for people,” Tucker says. “The voice of Heavens to Betsy was uncompromising, unfiltered and it never apologised for its rage and revenge-seeking.”

Tucker and Sawyer first met as middle schoolers in Eugene, Oregon, bonding over REM, the Cure, and Depeche Mode at sleepovers. They saw shows constantly – the Replacements, Firehose – and watched the music documentary Athens, GA: Inside/Out relentlessly. Their fixation on the Athens scene – including REM and the likes of B-52’s and Pylon – incited what Tucker calls a “pretty bonkers” and penniless cross-country train trip in summer 1990. The pair rented an apartment for a month to “study the scene”, bought a drum kit, watched Pylon through the window of the 40 Watt Club (they were too young to enter), and dubbed themselves Heavens to Betsy.

By the time Tucker arrived at Evergreen State College in Olympia that autumn, she had already crossed paths with Bratmobile singer and Girl Germs zinemaker Allison Wolfe, who hipped Tucker to the fiercely independent Oly scene. That year, Tucker made a film about local music and closely studied the bands she saw live: Beat Happening, Mecca Normal, Calamity Jane. Heavens to Betsy was still just an idea, but Tucker wrote lyrics to a song about menstruation and societal shame she called My Red Self. “I started telling people about our band when we hadn’t played a single show,” Tucker says. “Or had a practice. No songs either,” she laughs. “We had a concept.”

That’s an instructive blueprint. “You manifest it,” Sawyer offers.

“And believe in it,” Tucker adds. “You have to create the world before anything else, and cling to it. That’s true about every creative idea: you need to commit to that world. And once you do, then you can make it real for everyone else.”

When they were asked to play “Girl Night” at the International Pop Underground Convention, they anxiously accepted and Tucker sprang into action: many of the songs on their demo were written in her childhood bedroom. Fugazi’s Ian MacKaye was so impressed by Heavens to Betsy’s live debut that he sought them out to shake their hands.

“There was an openness to my voice that I think grabbed people right away,” Tucker says. “There wasn’t much filter between my emotions and my voice, so when I sang, it was really sad and angry at the same time. We kept our music really simple and focused. I wanted people to feel what I was feeling. People cried at that show. There was this movement of girls that were like, I need to talk about these things that we’re not supposed to talk about. I think my voice was just waiting for that door to open.”

At the centre of Baby’s Gone is a taut, unflinching song called My Secret in which Tucker lucidly blasts an abuser. She had been influenced by the directness of Bikini Kill frontperson Kathleen Hanna’s writing. “I felt brave because of what was happening around us,” she says. “It made me realise that I needed to let out my own feelings about things that had happened to me. It put me in the position of power.” Sawyer’s minimal, pounding beat “created this shield and weapon”, Tucker adds. “I was able to harness that into a song about being sexually abused. It turned the tables on everything, and it let go of everything, and it also freaked everyone out. It was incredible. It changed my life in a way. I was able to open a door to how maybe the rest of my life was gonna go. I didn’t need to hold on to those feelings any more.”

Heavens to Betsy’s songs were sometimes written in character, but informed by reality. The title track of Baby’s Gone narrates a young woman’s decision to have an abortion under conditions that leave her dead. “Back then, you couldn’t even say the word ‘abortion’, so there was a lot of euphemism around it,” Tucker says. “Young women had to deal with all of the consequences of heterosexual sex, which took all of the pressure off men in our society. I find that to be incredibly unfair.” Tucker wrote the song to ask, “What if the young woman who died having an abortion came back and wrote about her experience? What if a ghost came back and wrote the song? How would that make you feel?” She lets out a self-aware laugh.

“Connecting with your rage and your anger, in a way that lets it out – it feels important,” she adds, especially in light of the current political nightmares. “The past few years have been awful, and we really don’t have a way to process it. Liking things on my phone doesn’t cut it for me.”

The Baby’s Gone songs excavate trauma – “I want you to stay dead!” Tucker fumes at a memory – allowing the band’s one album, 1994’s grungier Calculated, to more explicitly claim power. “The first songs we wrote were really personal, and they were out of sheer necessity,” Tucker says. A few seem to describe vexed mother-daughter dynamics. “That relationship is always ripe for conflict,” she says. “Part of becoming a person in the world is differentiating yourself and saying, ‘No, I’m going to do things my way.’ Being a mom myself now, I’ve been on both sides of that, and it’s complicated.”

We’ve spoken for an hour and a half when Sawyer has to leave for a work meeting (she has a job at a pet supply company). Tucker and I keep chatting. The Heavens to Betsy reunion has offered an opportunity to revisit the music as well as to rekindle their friendship. “Getting a second chance feels like a real gift,” she says. “I’ve really enjoyed getting to know what Tracy’s life has been like and what we have in common.” When they drifted apart after Calculated came out, something they blame on having poor communication skills at that age, Tucker had already formed Sleater-Kinney alongside Carrie Brownstein, then guitarist in queercore band Excuse 17, who Heavens to Betsy had toured with.

Tucker sounds not especially fazed by where Heavens to Betsy might fit into modern music. But I mention Wednesday’s Karly Hartzman, and she joyfully recalls a Portugal festival where she heard her scream from stage. She also brings up Rodrigo’s Daisy Chain fest: “It’s both cool and terribly sad that we’re still holding a rock show to try and talk about our needs instead of having the kind of cultural, political, and economic power that would give us full equality.”

I ask about the lessons Tucker has gleaned from returning to this formative period of her life. “That courage you have as a young person to speak the truth and to find out what that means for you, that’s a really special thing to learn how to do, and it’s not always easy to maintain that when you’re becoming a mom and taking care of other people,” she says. “I do think there’s something really special about returning to Heavens to Betsy as my youngest goes off to college. I suddenly am rediscovering, what do I want, and who am I? There’s something very full circle about reconnecting with this voice that was like, ‘These are my feelings. This is my truth.’”

Baby’s Gone is released via Kill Rock Stars on 16 October. Heavens to Betsy tour the US from 17 October.

Lewes derailment: images show track defect before incident on hottest day

The Guardian Wed, 19 Aug 2026 14:45:03 GMT

Network Rail and Southern owner GTR apologise after investigators reveal picture of possible heat-buckled track

Rail operators have apologised after a report into last Thursday’s derailment in East Sussex found a track defect on the approach to where the train derailed on the hottest day of the year so far.

An interim report by the Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB) said CCTV images showed the “track geometry irregularity” existed before the incident near Lewes injured 30 people.

The watchdog published an image that appeared to show the track had buckled – something that can happen in high temperatures – before the Southern train derailed.

It said its investigation was taking weather conditions into account, as well as the status of the track, embankment, condition of the train and the effectiveness of any measures taken to mitigate the hot temperatures.

The report said there had been “a sustained period of hot and dry weather” and that the ambient air temperature at the time was about 27C, according to the nearest weather station to the site.

In a joint statement, Network Rail and Greater Thameslink Railway (GTR), which runs Southern, said they were “very sorry that this happened on our railway”.

“We also recognise the ongoing impact the incident has had on customers, local communities and railway colleagues,” said Lucy McAuliffe, Sussex route director at Network Rail, and John Whitehurst, chief executive at GTR.

“Safety is and will always remain our highest priority. While Britain’s railway is one of the safest in the world, when incidents like this occur it is essential that we understand exactly what happened and identify any lessons that can be learned.”

The stretch of railway between Lewes and Haywards Heath is scheduled to remain closed until at least the end of service on 26 August. That will give time for the train to be recovered – a complex job involving the derailed carriages being lifted by crane – and for recovery teams to make sure evidence is preserved.

The incident happened on 13 August amid the UK’s fifth heatwave of the summer, during which two trains derailed in less than 24 hours. The second derailment occurred on Friday when the rear carriages of a Greater Anglia train came off the track “in an upright position” at Wickford railway station in Essex, with no reported injuries.

The embankment on which the railway sits near the Lewes derailment site is made of clay, meaning it is “sensitive to variations in water content and may undergo movement as moisture levels change”, the RAIB said.

It added that “although, at this stage, there is no evidence to indicate that a significant embankment slip occurred before the accident, there is evidence that some movement had previously taken place”.

RAIB investigators said they had received “several reports of rough riding” from passengers on other trains in the same location.

It is understood that investigation teams still consider the inquiry to be in its very early days and the final report may not be published for a year or longer.

The Office of Rail and Road (ORR). said it was also “investigating the circumstances of the incident” but declined to comment further. Unlike the RAIB, the ORR’s remit is to look into potential “breaches of health and safety law” and it has the power to prosecute on those grounds.

The train was travelling at about 65mph – within the 70mph speed limit – as it approached the site of the incident, with about 150 people onboard.

Three carriages ended up on their side, trapping passengers and injuring 30 people, including 20 who required hospital treatment, the RAIB said. “Significant damage was caused to the train and to railway infrastructure,” the watchdog added.

James MacCleary, the Liberal Democrat MP for Lewes, said the early findings “raise serious concerns”, and the fault on the track was “deeply concerning”.

“I travel this line very regularly and reported to the authorities just how bumpy this section of track had become. We cannot assume that this is related, but that makes the current findings even more troubling.”

The Department for Transport said: “Safety remains the absolute priority across our rail network, and we will ensure the industry acts on any findings in the Rail Accident Investigation Branch’s full report when published.”

US justice department defends prosecution of James Comey over ‘8647’ seashell post

The Guardian Wed, 19 Aug 2026 14:27:57 GMT

Justice department claims there’s ‘no dispute’ over whether ex-FBI head’s post could be read as a threat against Trump

The US Department of Justice has defended its prosecution of former FBI director James Comey, claiming in new court documents there is “no serious dispute” that his social media post last year featuring a photo of seashells arranged to read “8647” could be interpreted as a threat against Donald Trump.

“There is no serious dispute that an objective viewer of Comey’s post could read it to mean ‘Kill President Trump’,” prosecutors wrote in a document filed on Tuesday in response to efforts by Comey’s efforts to have the case dismissed.

Comey was indicted in April after a grand jury in North Carolina charged him with making a threat against the US president and transmitting that threat, via social media, across state lines, over an image he posted on Instagram while vacationing in North Carolina last May.

In the photo, the seashells were arranged to read “8647”, which the president’s allies and supporters quickly denounced as a threat against Trump. The number “86” is often used as shorthand to mean to get rid of or remove something, while Trump is the 47th US president.

Comey deleted the photo after the uproar, saying he didn’t know that it could be interpreted as a violent threat. “It never occurred to me, but I oppose violence of any kind so I took the post down,” he said.

In the court documents filed earlier this week, prosecutors with the eastern district of North Carolina continued to argue the post was a “coded message to his followers meaning ‘kill’ or ‘get rid of’ President Trump”.

Comey has denied the charges against him and his lawyers have asked the judge to dismiss the case, arguing that the post was protected speech and did not amount to a “true threat” against the president.

“The indictment alleges that Mr Comey’s ‘86 47’ post constitutes a ‘true threat; on the President’s life,” Comey’s lawyers wrote in a filing last month. “That claim is contradicted by every possible source of meaning: dictionaries, context, precedent, and common sense. ‘86’ simply means ‘get rid of’ or ‘eject’ and has no violent connotation except in the most uncommon usages.”

Comey’s lawyers have argued that “in this context, no reasonable observer would understand the phrase ‘86 47’ to connote violence at all – let alone to threaten that Mr Comey personally would commit violence against the President”.

Comey’s lawyers have also said the case should be dismissed for “vindictive and selective prosecution” and have said the indictment is “not based on a goodfaith application of the law to the facts; instead, it effectuates a yearslong campaign by the President to use the criminal process to punish Mr Comey for his protected speech and because of the President’s deep-seated animosity”.

Trump has long feuded with Comey since his handling of the investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election while he was FBI director.

Last year, the justice department also indicted Comey in a separate case, alleging that he had lied to Congress. But those charges were later thrown out after a judge ruled the prosecutor handling the case was unlawfully appointed.
